nodes.summary: Unify multimodal understanding, generation, simulation and action interfaces in a shared model family.
nodes.definition: Cosmos 3 introduces an omnimodal world-model family with a mixture-of-transformers architecture that can process and generate language, images, video, audio and action sequences. The framework supports understanding, visual generation, forward or inverse dynamics and policy-related interfaces through different input-output configurations. This is a unification of capabilities within a model family, not proof that every configuration is equally reliable for every robot. Reported rankings and benchmark results must be tied to their task, model tier and evaluation date.
nodes.example: One configuration can answer a visual question about a manipulation scene; another can condition future video on actions; another can generate robot actions. These modes share a framework but have different outputs and validation criteria. A good language answer does not establish accurate rollouts, and realistic video does not establish successful motor execution.

nodes.summary: Learn interactive generative environments with latent actions from unlabeled videos.
nodes.definition: Genie learns action-controllable generative environments from videos without ground-truth action labels. A video tokenizer compresses observations, a latent-action model infers discrete interaction variables between frames, and an autoregressive dynamics model predicts subsequent tokens conditioned on those variables. The learned controls allow interactive generation from an initial image. The main demonstrations concern visual environments and learned latent controls; these latent actions are not automatically robot torques, and generated interaction is not a validated physical model of a robot.
nodes.example: Use two consecutive video frames to infer an unobserved latent action. Train dynamics to predict the next video tokens given that latent and context. At generation time a user selects a latent action to influence the world. Mapping that latent to a physical motor command requires additional grounding and validation.
nodes.role_en: This adjacent branch explains action discovery from video and interactive generative simulation. It helps distinguish video controllability from robot-specific action-conditioned dynamics.

nodes.definition: Genie 2 is an officially announced foundation world model for generating playable three-dimensional visual environments from an initial image. The announcement describes action-controllable interaction for people or agents and demonstrations of scene consistency and varied visual behavior. The source used here is an official research blog rather than an accompanying fully specified public paper. Therefore undisclosed architecture details, model parameter counts and independent physical-accuracy guarantees are not inferred. Its robotics relevance is as an adjacent environment-generation direction for embodied-agent training.
nodes.example: Provide an image of a room and use keyboard or mouse-style inputs to move through its generated environment. Observe whether objects and layout persist when the camera turns. This can demonstrate visual interaction and memory, but it does not measure joint torque accuracy, contact forces or a manipulation policy success rate on hardware.

nodes.summary: Use autoregressive Transformers as sample-efficient learned visual environments.
nodes.definition: IRIS learns a world model using a discrete visual autoencoder and an autoregressive Transformer, then trains an actor-critic through generated interaction. The tokenizer converts images into discrete symbols, allowing sequence prediction to model their temporal evolution with actions and feedback. The work investigates sample efficiency under the Atari 100k protocol. Its relevance is architectural: tokenization, long-context sequence modeling and imagination-based behavior can be compared with stochastic latent-state or diffusion world models. It does not provide direct robot-hardware evidence.
nodes.example: Encode a game frame into discrete visual tokens, append action context and predict the next token sequence plus feedback. Roll the model forward to train an actor in generated experience. Compression errors can remove task-relevant visual details, which motivates comparisons with pixel-oriented diffusion prediction.
nodes.role_en: IRIS provides an autoregressive-token branch between recurrent latent world models and diffusion observation models. It is included as a methodological foundation adjacent to robot learning.

nodes.summary: Use diffusion observation prediction to retain visual details during imagination-based RL.
nodes.definition: DIAMOND learns an action-conditioned diffusion observation model and trains a reinforcement-learning policy inside the generated environment. Its motivation is that compact discrete representations can lose visual details important to control. The paper studies design choices that make few-step diffusion prediction practical for repeated world-model rollouts. Reward and termination feedback are modeled alongside observations for behavior learning. The principal results are Atari and a neural game-engine demonstration, so transferring the architecture to robots requires suitable actions, observations and physically matched evaluation.
nodes.example: Given recent frames and an action, denoise a predicted next frame while preserving details needed to decide the next action. Repeat to generate an imagined episode and improve the policy. A sharp image that moves the wrong object can still mislead the policy, so visual fidelity and action/outcome accuracy are separate requirements.
nodes.role_en: DIAMOND is a clear pixel/diffusion comparison to JEPA latent prediction and discrete-token world models. Its game evidence is methodologically useful but does not establish physical robot reliability.

nodes.summary: A predictive latent objective matches a predicted representation of a target to an encoded target representation.
nodes.definition: A predictive latent objective matches a predicted representation of a target to an encoded target representation. The conditioning specifies what is being predicted: a masked image region, a video region or an action-conditioned future state. Training need not reconstruct RGB pixels or use explicit negative examples. The target representation, masking and anti-collapse mechanism determine which information can be retained. This objective alone permits degenerate constant representations unless additional structure or regularization prevents them; successful prediction is not automatically evidence of physical accuracy.
nodes.example: For image prediction, context consists of visible patches and the condition identifies missing target locations. For robot dynamics, context can be the current latent state and the condition contains an action sequence. Both predict representations, but only the latter explicitly evaluates motor consequences. Compare the input, target and conditioning before calling two models equivalent.

nodes.summary: Stop-gradient prevents a target feature from receiving derivatives through a specified loss path.
nodes.definition: Stop-gradient prevents a target feature from receiving derivatives through a specified loss path. An exponential-moving-average target encoder instead defines how target parameters are updated over training iterations. These are different operations: one controls differentiation and the other updates weights outside the optimizer gradient rule. A slowly changing target can stabilize representation learning, but neither stop-gradient nor EMA alone is a universal anti-collapse proof. Some predictive methods use frozen targets or explicit distribution regularizers rather than this exact EMA design.
nodes.example: With momentum 0.99, old target weight 1 and online weight 2, the new target weight is 1.01. During backpropagation, the loss still updates the online encoder and predictor, while the target branch is detached. The EMA assignment later changes target weights using the online values; it is not an Adam gradient update.
nodes.role_en: I-JEPA and video JEPA use target-encoder mechanisms to supply prediction targets. This concept is reusable with DINO-style teacher/student learning, while LeWorldModel should not be assumed to inherit an EMA target merely because it is JEPA-based.

nodes.title: 概率集成与轨迹采样控制
nodes.summary: Use probabilistic model ensembles with trajectory sampling for sample-efficient continuous control.
nodes.definition: PETS learns an ensemble of probabilistic neural dynamics models and propagates their uncertainty with sampled trajectories during planning. Each model predicts a state-change distribution, while differences between members reflect uncertainty associated with limited training coverage. Candidate action sequences are evaluated using particles and sampling-based optimization in an MPC loop. The method explicitly studies uncertainty-aware planning rather than treating a single deterministic model prediction as certain. Ensemble disagreement is useful but is not automatically a calibrated probability of failure on every unseen state.
nodes.example: For each candidate action sequence, propagate several state particles while sampling ensemble members and transition noise according to the chosen trajectory-sampling variant. Compare predicted returns across these particles, refine candidates with CEM and execute the first action. When models disagree about an unfamiliar contact state, the planner sees a broader outcome distribution than a single mean prediction would provide.
nodes.role_en: PETS connects probabilistic regression, epistemic versus aleatoric uncertainty, ensembles and MPC. It is a practical state-space model-based control foundation that complements representation-focused world-model papers.

Candidate action sequences are evaluated using particles and sampling-based optimization in an MPC loop. The method explicitly studies uncertainty-aware planning rather than treating a single deterministic model prediction as certain. Ensemble disagreement is useful but is not automatically a calibrated probability of failure on every unseen state.

nodes.summary: Use short model-generated rollouts branched from real data to balance sample reuse against model bias.
nodes.definition: MBPO studies how much to use a learned dynamics model when improving a policy. Its practical algorithm starts short synthetic rollouts from states sampled from real replay, then mixes generated transitions with real data for off-policy actor-critic updates. This separates modeling from behavior optimization and reduces reliance on long open-loop imagined trajectories. The theoretical analysis motivates the tradeoff between additional synthetic experience and model bias; its monotonic-improvement analysis should not be treated as an unconditional guarantee for an arbitrary learned neural simulator.
nodes.example: Choose a state from a real replay buffer, run the current policy through the learned ensemble for only a few steps, and store those imagined transitions separately. Use many such short branches to train the policy. Restarting from recorded states limits the distance traveled through a potentially inaccurate model, although distribution shift can still occur within each branch.
nodes.role_en: MBPO explains why longer model rollouts are not always better. It connects learned dynamics to off-policy optimization and provides a useful comparison with latent imagination agents that use different state and gradient pathways.

nodes.summary: Learn visual interaction simulation from diverse datasets and use it to train embodied policies.
nodes.definition: UniSim learns a generative visual simulator of interactions by combining datasets that contribute different forms of coverage: diverse objects, camera motion, human behavior or robot actions. The model can be conditioned on high-level language or low-level action descriptions to generate visual outcomes. The paper explores using simulated experience to train high-level and low-level policies and evaluates selected transfers to the real world. Its universal-simulator framing is an objective for broad interaction modeling, not a demonstrated replacement for every physical simulation subsystem.
nodes.example: An image dataset can supply object diversity while a robot dataset supplies action-conditioned movement examples. Train one conditional generator on the combined interfaces, then request a future showing a drawer opening from a current view. A policy trained using these generated interactions must still be tested on the relevant hardware and task; visual plausibility alone cannot establish the accuracy of hidden forces.
nodes.role_en: UniSim is an important bridge from general video generation to robot-policy training through learned interaction simulation. It motivates separate evaluation of visual quality, action controllability and real policy transfer.

nodes.summary: Use language-conditioned video plans as a shared planning interface, then ground them into task-specific actions.
nodes.definition: UniPi formulates a policy through a text-conditioned video plan and a separate action-grounding mechanism. The generator is explicitly conditioned on the starting observation, and temporal super-resolution refines sparse coarse plans into more detailed sequences. A task-specific inverse-dynamics adapter translates visual transitions into executable actions. This separation allows video and language data to contribute planning knowledge across environments, while the action interface still needs environment-specific data. A compelling robot video plan should not be confused with demonstrated physical execution of that plan.
nodes.example: Provide an image and the goal to place an object left of another object. Generate sparse intermediate frames, refine them in time and infer control actions with an adapter trained for the target environment. Execute with observation feedback. The same visual planner can propose plans for different environments, but a control mapping from one robot cannot automatically be sent to another embodiment.
nodes.role_en: UniPi connects generative video planning, language goals, temporal hierarchy and inverse dynamics. It helps distinguish planning future observations from learning an action-conditioned forward simulator such as UniSim.

nodes.summary: Combine causal sequence prediction and diffusion by independently corrupting token positions.
nodes.definition: Diffusion Forcing trains a causal sequence model to denoise tokens whose noise levels are sampled independently across the sequence. This permits observed history and uncertain future positions to have different corruption levels, combining variable-length autoregressive generation with diffusion-style guidance. At sampling time, different causal noise schedules support robust rollout and planning. The framework is broader than one robot policy architecture: the paper evaluates video prediction, decision-making, robot-related tasks and time-series settings under distinct configurations. Long generation alone does not establish long-horizon physical accuracy.
nodes.example: Keep past observations near the clean end of the diffusion schedule while initializing future tokens with stronger noise. Denoise future positions conditionally, without requiring every past token to be fully corrupted again. Guidance can favor desirable trajectories. Training with independent noise levels teaches the model to handle many combinations of reliable and uncertain token positions.
nodes.role_en: This paper bridges next-token prediction, full-sequence diffusion, causal conditioning and guidance-based planning. It is useful for understanding flexible-horizon world models without treating every diffusion sampler as an identical temporal model.

nodes.title: 行为克隆
nodes.summary: Behavior cloning learns a policy by fitting demonstrated actions conditioned on observations and task context.
nodes.definition: Behavior cloning learns a policy by fitting demonstrated actions conditioned on observations and task context. A probabilistic policy minimizes negative log likelihood; squared regression is a special modeling choice rather than the only possible behavior-cloning loss. The demonstrations determine which states and strategies are covered. Closed-loop execution can visit states absent from demonstrations, making recovery behavior and distribution shift important. Behavior cloning does not require a learned transition model or a scalar task reward, although it can be combined with either in a larger training pipeline.
nodes.example: Record images and gripper commands while a person teleoperates object pickup. Fit the action distribution for each recorded observation. If the deployed gripper misses, it may see a configuration not present in successful demonstrations; high demonstration likelihood alone does not establish recovery ability.
nodes.role_en: This is the supervised-policy foundation shared by ACT, diffusion policies and many VLAs. It is distinct from using a world model to search actions at inference, and from improving a policy using autonomous reward-labeled experience.

nodes.summary: A vision-language model combines image information with language context to support tasks such as captioning and visual question answering.
nodes.definition: A vision-language model combines image information with language context to support tasks such as captioning and visual question answering. A vision-language-action model adds an interface that predicts executable robot actions. That interface can use discrete action tokens, continuous regression, diffusion or flow matching. Visual-language understanding and physical action grounding are separate requirements: knowing what a mug is does not automatically specify safe joint commands. Robot demonstrations, action conventions and embodiment information connect pretrained representations to a particular control interface.
nodes.example: The instruction pick up the red cup conditions a model on an image containing several cups. A VLM can identify the intended object; a VLA must additionally predict actions in the robot coordinate and control convention. A correct object description can coexist with an unsuccessful grasp.
nodes.role_en: This reusable node connects multimodal pretraining to RT-2, OpenVLA, the pi family, GR00T and Gemini Robotics. It should not be interpreted as evidence that every VLA explicitly predicts future world states.

nodes.title: 动作分块
nodes.summary: Action chunking predicts several consecutive control actions from one policy inference.
nodes.definition: Action chunking predicts several consecutive control actions from one policy inference. It changes the temporal interface between a model and its controller, reducing the number of policy calls required to execute a trajectory. Chunk length, executed prefix length, observation latency and replanning frequency are different settings. A long chunk can reduce inference overhead but makes execution less reactive when used without new feedback. Chunk prediction is compatible with Transformer, variational, diffusion and flow-based policies and does not itself identify which action distribution is learned.
nodes.example: At a fifty-hertz controller rate, fifty predicted actions describe one second of desired control. Executing all fifty before looking again produces a different closed-loop system from executing ten actions and recomputing. The same network can therefore behave differently under different chunk scheduling choices.
nodes.role_en: ACT makes action chunking explicit; many later generalist policies also use it. The concept connects temporal modeling to deployment latency, RTC and asynchronous inference, rather than representing a full world model by itself.

nodes.title: 条件流匹配
nodes.summary: Flow matching trains a vector field that transports samples along a specified probability path.
nodes.definition: Flow matching trains a vector field that transports samples along a specified probability path. Conditional flow matching supplies observations or task context to that field. The displayed linear interpolation between independent noise and demonstrated actions is an illustrative conditional path: the regression target is the displacement along that path. At inference, a numerical differential-equation solver integrates the learned field from a noise distribution toward the data distribution. The number of integration evaluations controls a computational budget and is distinct from robot control frequency.
nodes.example: For a scalar demonstrated action of two and sampled noise of minus one, the linear path at generative time one half equals one half, and its target velocity is three. A conditioned neural network learns this velocity from many such examples before generating new action chunks.
nodes.role_en: Flow matching is the continuous-action generation component used in pi0 and related VLAs. Its differential-equation interpretation adds a direct connection to calculus, numerical integration and runtime model evaluations.

nodes.title: 离散动作词元
nodes.summary: Action tokenization maps continuous control values or trajectories into discrete symbols that a sequence model can predict.
nodes.definition: Action tokenization maps continuous control values or trajectories into discrete symbols that a sequence model can predict. Simple binning discretizes each action coordinate independently; compression-based tokenizers instead encode structure across an action sequence. The decoder maps tokens back to the required continuous control convention. Token count, precision and temporal resolution affect both learning and inference. Autoregressive token prediction normally incurs sequential decoding work, so a shorter representation can change latency without changing the physical duration covered by the generated actions.
nodes.example: A seven-dimensional action discretized independently into one token per coordinate requires seven tokens for one step. A chunk of many steps becomes much longer. A sequence-level tokenizer can exploit smoothness, but quantization error must still be assessed on precise contact tasks.
nodes.role_en: RT-2 and OpenVLA expose actions to language-style sequence training; FAST changes the tokenizer. These are alternative action-generation mechanisms to continuous diffusion or flow heads, not a claim that language tokens simulate physics.

nodes.summary: A differentiable learned dynamics model predicts state transitions with operations through which derivatives can be propagated.
nodes.definition: A differentiable learned dynamics model predicts state transitions with operations through which derivatives can be propagated. A policy can be optimized by differentiating an objective along model-generated trajectories. The model is a fitted surrogate; the physical simulator or real robot supplying training transitions need not be differentiable. Gradients can become misleading when model errors accumulate or the optimizer exploits unsupported transitions. Short rollout horizons, model updates and feedback are practical controls but do not make a learned model an exact replacement for contact physics.
nodes.example: Collect state-action-next-state transitions from a standard rigid-body simulator. Fit a smooth neural predictor. During one policy update hold predictor weights fixed and differentiate the imagined reward with respect to policy parameters. New simulator samples can subsequently update the predictor without differentiating simulator internals.
nodes.role_en: SuperMimic uses this route for humanoid tracking-policy training. It connects Jacobians, chain rules and BPTT to control, and separates a small state predictor from a large visual scene-generation model.

nodes.title: 异步策略执行
nodes.summary: Asynchronous execution overlaps inference for a future chunk with execution of currently available actions.
nodes.definition: Asynchronous execution overlaps inference for a future chunk with execution of currently available actions. This can remove pauses caused by waiting for each inference call. It also creates a consistency problem: by the time a new chunk arrives, the robot has moved and its initial actions may already be obsolete. Scheduling, observation timestamps and chunk alignment therefore affect behavior. The idealized timing expression concerns overlap only; it does not guarantee stable motion or successful feedback control.
nodes.example: A controller executes the remaining two hundred milliseconds of an old chunk while a server generates the next chunk. If inference takes one hundred milliseconds, computation can overlap. The new chunk still must be aligned to the future switch time rather than replayed from the observation timestamp.
nodes.role_en: RTC explicitly handles chunk consistency for flow policies, while SmolVLA supplies an asynchronous deployment stack. This links action models to systems latency and control semantics.

nodes.title: 跨本体数据与动作接口
nodes.summary: Cross-embodiment learning uses data from robots with different bodies, sensors or control interfaces.
nodes.definition: Cross-embodiment learning uses data from robots with different bodies, sensors or control interfaces. Shared training requires identifying which features and action meanings can be aligned and which need embodiment-specific adapters. Equal numerical action dimensions do not imply equal physical meaning: joint targets, Cartesian deltas and force commands have different semantics. Dataset standardization, units, coordinate conventions and normalization are prerequisites for meaningful transfer. A common policy can share representations while retaining per-robot output heads or fine-tuning steps.
nodes.example: A delta pose for one arm cannot be copied directly into another robot joint-target interface. The policy or its adapter must translate between those conventions, respecting limits and frames. A successful transfer experiment must specify which target-robot demonstrations and calibration data were used.
nodes.role_en: Open X-Embodiment, Octo, OpenVLA and later robot foundation models all depend on explicit cross-robot interfaces. This is an engineering and learning issue, not merely concatenating more episodes.

nodes.title: ACT 动作分块 Transformer
nodes.summary: Predict temporally coherent action chunks to learn precise bimanual skills from limited demonstrations.
nodes.definition: ACT learns fine-grained bimanual manipulation from teleoperated demonstrations by predicting chunks of joint commands with a Transformer conditional variational model. Images and current joint state condition the decoder; a training encoder summarizes demonstrated future actions into a latent. At deployment the learned decoder produces actions without access to future demonstrations. Temporal aggregation combines overlapping chunk predictions. The method is a policy rather than a transition predictor, although its temporal abstraction addresses the same compounding-error problem that motivates several planning and world-model approaches.
nodes.example: For battery insertion, cameras observe the battery and socket while joint readings specify the current arm configuration. ACT predicts a short sequence of joint targets rather than only the next target. Repeated observation and chunk prediction maintain feedback; the paper tests whether this enables precise behavior with a small demonstration set.
nodes.role_en: ACT is a precursor for action-chunk interfaces and a strong task-specific imitation baseline. Its future actions must not be confused with future-state predictions from a world model.

paper.inference: Decode a chunk from current observation and joint state; aggregate overlapping predictions during feedback execution.
paper.evaluation: Real bimanual fine manipulation and simulated transfer/insertion; task-specific success rates.
paper.scale: Low-cost ALOHA demonstrations; reported examples use about ten minutes of data. Total parameter count not independently summarized here.
paper.limitations: Task-specific demonstrations and camera/control conventions matter; this is not an open-world task planner or physics model.

nodes.explain: ACT learns fine-grained bimanual manipulation from teleoperated demonstrations by predicting chunks of joint commands with a Transformer conditional variational model. Images and current joint state condition the decoder; a training encoder summarizes demonstrated future actions into a latent. At deployment the learned decoder produces actions without access to future demonstrations. Temporal aggregation combines overlapping chunk predictions. The method is a policy rather than a transition predictor, although its temporal abstraction addresses the same compounding-error problem that motivates several planning and world-model approaches.
nodes.role: ACT is a precursor for action-chunk interfaces and a strong task-specific imitation baseline. Its future actions must not be confused with future-state predictions from a world model.

nodes.title: 扩散策略
nodes.summary: Model multimodal action sequences using conditional diffusion and receding-horizon execution.
nodes.definition: Diffusion Policy represents an observation-conditioned action distribution by iterative denoising. Rather than predicting an average action at each step, it can model multiple coherent action sequences. Visual observations condition a denoiser implemented with temporal convolutional or Transformer variants, and generated action chunks are executed with receding-horizon feedback. The denoising training target concerns robot actions, not image pixels or next physical state. Consequently, using diffusion does not make this policy a world model; the modeled variable and the inference interface determine that distinction.
nodes.example: A robot can move around an obstacle on either side. Independent average actions may point toward the obstacle, while a sampled action sequence can remain consistent with one route. The policy observes the scene again after executing part of the chunk, rather than assuming the entire imagined action sequence remains appropriate.
nodes.role_en: This provides a key generative-policy branch parallel to ID-WM. Both use denoising machinery, but Diffusion Policy generates actions and ID-WM high-level diffusion generates local future states.

paper.limitations: Sampling cost and task distribution remain important; it does not explicitly verify future physical feasibility.
paper.evidence_level: Primary paper and official project documentation

nodes.title: RT-1 机器人 Transformer
nodes.summary: Demonstrate a scalable task-agnostic robot Transformer trained on broad real robot data.
nodes.definition: RT-1 studies scalable real-world robot policy learning from a large multi-task demonstration collection. Language-conditioned visual features are compressed into tokens and processed by a Transformer to predict discretized control actions. Its central result concerns how data diversity and model capacity support task generalization in one robot platform setting. The model directly returns actions rather than simulating consequences for a separate planner. RT-1 therefore supplies an important policy-learning predecessor to later VLAs, while its own pretraining recipe should not be retroactively described as the web-scale VLM adaptation used in RT-2.
nodes.example: A mobile manipulator receives pick up the coke can and a history of camera observations. The network emits arm, gripper and base-related control tokens. Evaluation varies instructions and environmental conditions to check whether the learned policy transfers beyond its demonstrated combinations.
nodes.role_en: RT-1 anchors the language-conditioned robot Transformer lineage. It connects visual tokens and supervised action prediction before the introduction of web-knowledge transfer in RT-2.

paper.inference: Use observation history and instruction to predict tokenized controls in a closed loop.
paper.evaluation: Real-world task generalization, robustness and ablation evaluations.
paper.scale: The original collection reports roughly 130,000 episodes and 700-plus tasks; the model is about 35M parameters.
paper.limitations: Specific embodiments, task distribution and data collection restrict conclusions; not an explicit dynamics model.
paper.evidence_level: Primary paper and official project documentation

nodes.title: RT-2 视觉语言动作模型
nodes.summary: Transfer internet-scale visual-language knowledge into direct robot action prediction.
nodes.definition: RT-2 adapts pretrained vision-language models into robot policies by representing robot actions as text-like tokens. Co-fine-tuning mixes robot trajectories with internet-scale visual-language tasks so the model retains semantic knowledge while learning physical action outputs. At inference generated action tokens are decoded into robot controls. The paper evaluates novel objects, symbols and instruction reasoning, showing a route for transferring web-trained semantics to manipulation. Its semantic capabilities are not equivalent to an explicit simulator, and recognizing a useful object remains different from executing a physically reliable manipulation.
nodes.example: A robot is asked to pick the extinct animal from several objects, or choose an object that could serve as an improvised hammer. The language-image backbone can use concepts learned outside robot demonstrations, while the action decoder converts that interpretation into a familiar robot control interface.
nodes.role_en: RT-2 establishes the named VLA recipe of co-training web and robot data through a shared token prediction interface. It is a direct methodological development beyond RT-1.

nodes.title: Open X-Embodiment 与 RT-X
nodes.summary: Establish broad cross-embodiment data sharing and evaluate positive transfer in generalist policies.
nodes.definition: Open X-Embodiment combines robot learning datasets from many institutions and embodiments and evaluates shared policy training through RT-X models. The scientific question is whether mixing compatible robot experience produces positive transfer instead of interference. The contribution includes standardized data access and cross-embodiment policy experiments, not merely a larger neural network. Dataset versions and mixtures evolve, so a named corpus does not uniquely specify training input. Observations, actions, language annotations and sampling weights must be documented to reproduce a particular policy result.
nodes.example: A training batch can include tabletop arm data from one lab and mobile manipulation data from another. Standardized records simplify loading, but the meaning of actions and camera observations still differs. Experiments compare policies trained with and without the additional robot data to isolate positive transfer.
nodes.role_en: This is a data and model foundation for Octo, OpenVLA and many later VLAs. It connects dataset engineering to transfer across bodies rather than implying that all embodiments can share raw controls.

nodes.title: Octo 通用机器人策略
nodes.summary: Offer open generalist policies with efficient adaptation to new sensors and action interfaces.
nodes.definition: Octo is an open generalist manipulation policy designed for flexible task definitions and observation or action interfaces. A Transformer processes tokenized observations and language or image goals, while a diffusion head models action chunks. The model is pretrained on a broad robot dataset and adapted with task-specific data to new robots or sensors. Its architectural modularity is part of the contribution: adding or replacing observation and output interfaces supports different deployment settings. Octo is a conditional action policy; it does not require rendering a predicted physical future before choosing actions.
nodes.example: A base Octo policy can be fine-tuned from one arm setup to another with a different camera combination or action dimension. A goal can be given as language or an image. Evaluation must say which robot data were used for adaptation instead of labeling every target-platform rollout as zero-shot.
nodes.role_en: Octo is a compact, reproducible alternative to VLM-token VLAs and a bridge from Open X-Embodiment to diffusion-based generalist action prediction.

nodes.title: OpenVLA 开源视觉语言动作模型
nodes.summary: Release a strong open VLA and a reproducible fine-tuning ecosystem.
nodes.definition: OpenVLA is an open vision-language-action model that adapts a pretrained multimodal backbone for robot manipulation. It combines visual features with a language model and predicts discretized action tokens using demonstration supervision. Its release includes weights and a PyTorch training pipeline, enabling controlled fine-tuning and deployment research. The paper studies generalist manipulation and parameter-efficient adaptation rather than claiming a complete dynamics simulator. Later OpenVLA extensions can change action decoding, latency and chunking; those changes should be identified separately from the original model.
nodes.example: A model pretrained on multiple robot datasets can be evaluated directly on supported platforms or fine-tuned for a new Franka task. The visual-language representation identifies instruction-relevant objects, while action tokens encode the motion convention used by that deployment. An out-of-box rollout and a target-task fine-tuned rollout are different evidence levels.
nodes.role_en: OpenVLA is a key open VLA reference for comparing token-based actions, fine-tuning cost and cross-embodiment transfer against flow and diffusion policies.

nodes.title: π0 视觉语言动作流模型
nodes.summary: Combine large visual-language pretraining with flow-based continuous action generation for general robot control.
nodes.definition: pi0 combines a pretrained vision-language backbone with a continuous action expert trained by flow matching. The model conditions on images, language and robot state to generate action chunks across multiple robot platforms. Continuous action generation supports high-frequency dexterous behavior without representing every control coordinate as an independent text token. Its training mixes robot data and builds on visual-language pretraining, but the model directly produces a policy output rather than solving a separate trajectory search with a learned transition model.
nodes.example: For folding a shirt, camera images and joint state condition a vector field over a future action chunk. Starting from noise, integration generates the chunk, which is executed through the robot interface. Repeating this process supplies feedback; the generated chunk is a sequence of controls, not a prediction of future shirt pixels.
nodes.role_en: pi0 connects VLM grounding to flow matching and high-frequency robot actions. It is the direct architectural foundation for the later pi0.5 family described in the official work.

nodes.title: FAST 高效动作词元化
nodes.summary: Enable effective autoregressive robot action learning through frequency-domain action compression.
nodes.definition: FAST changes how action chunks are represented for autoregressive VLA training. It transforms temporal action sequences into frequency coefficients, quantizes them and compresses the resulting symbols using byte-pair encoding. Smooth structure can therefore be represented with fewer tokens than independent per-step bins. The model still predicts discrete outputs, but the tokenizer is designed for high-frequency dexterous trajectories. Tokenization quality trades off compression, reconstruction error and downstream control, so a token-count reduction is not by itself a physical success guarantee.
nodes.example: A fifty-step joint trajectory often varies smoothly. Independent binning emits a long sequence even when most temporal detail is low frequency. FAST compresses the transform coefficients, and a decoder reconstructs a continuous chunk. Precision should be checked on the reconstructed controls and actual robot tasks, not only on compression ratio.
nodes.role_en: FAST provides a distinct action-representation branch from pi0 flow generation. The pi0-FAST model demonstrates how action token design affects VLM transfer and training efficiency.

nodes.title: π0.5 开放环境泛化
nodes.summary: Improve environmental and semantic generalization by jointly training on diverse supervision sources.
nodes.definition: pi0.5 extends the pi0 line by co-training on heterogeneous robot and non-robot supervision to support generalization to new environments. It combines physical action learning with high-level semantic and task-structure information. The official work emphasizes mobile manipulation in homes that were not used for scene-specific training. Open-world generalization here denotes those evaluated environmental variations; it should not be interpreted as solving every unseen task or eliminating the need for robot action data. The paper and release should be distinguished from later memory and reinforcement-learning extensions.
nodes.example: A mobile manipulator is asked to clean a new kitchen. It must infer a sequence of subtasks, identify familiar object categories in a different layout and execute learned skills. A task can fail at semantic choice, navigation or contact execution; an overall successful example does not identify which component generalized.

nodes.title: π*0.6 从经验中学习
nodes.summary: Use experience and corrections to improve VLA reliability and task throughput.
nodes.definition: pi-star-0.6 applies RECAP, reinforcement learning with experience and corrections via advantage-conditioned policies, to improve a generalist VLA beyond demonstration-only training. Demonstrations establish task behavior, human corrections address observed mistakes, and autonomous experience provides additional outcomes for improvement. The resulting model is the RL-trained pi-star variant, while pi0.6 denotes the underlying model family. Treating these names as interchangeable hides the training change that the paper studies. Its main evidence concerns task reliability and throughput in repeated real-world execution.
nodes.example: On espresso preparation, a policy can recover from conditions absent in successful demonstrations. Data from its own attempts and interventions can improve behavior on those visited states. Evaluating an all-day run tests sustained reliability differently from measuring the error of a single predicted action.
nodes.role_en: This connects policy imitation to reward/value concepts and distribution shift. It does not require differentiating a learned world model in the SuperMimic manner.

nodes.title: π0.7 可引导通用模型
nodes.summary: Train a steerable generalist model using rich context to disambiguate diverse robot behavior.
nodes.definition: pi0.7 studies a steerable generalist VLA trained with varied multimodal context. Prompts can specify not only task identity but how a task should be executed, including visual subgoals, desired duration or strategy-related information. Such context helps disambiguate heterogeneous behaviors in large data mixtures. The official work reports improved generalization and compositional behavior, including combinations not demonstrated on a target robot. These are evaluated capabilities rather than a formal guarantee of arbitrary skill composition, and the visual subgoal interface should be distinguished from a dynamics model that proves reachability.
nodes.example: A reasoning system can supply a visual arrangement showing where objects should end up, alongside a language instruction. The policy then generates low-level actions conditioned on that context. A visual plan that looks plausible can still fail physically; task execution and adaptation data remain necessary evaluation evidence.
nodes.role_en: pi0.7 connects VLA control to visual steering and richer contextual conditioning. It illustrates a current bridge between explicit goals, generative observations and direct action policies.

nodes.title: MEM 多尺度具身记忆
nodes.summary: Combine visual short-term and language long-term memory for sustained robot tasks.
nodes.definition: Multi-Scale Embodied Memory equips a VLA with short-horizon visual history and longer-horizon abstract language memory. The short-term encoder preserves recent motion and interaction information, while language records task progress and relevant events beyond the raw-image window. The method jointly reasons about what to do and what to retain. Memory helps partial observability but can introduce causal confusion if irrelevant past information creates spurious shortcuts. The system therefore addresses a specific architectural and training problem rather than assuming that unlimited context automatically improves robot control.
nodes.example: During kitchen cleanup, an object can leave the camera view after being placed in a drawer. A recent image window no longer contains the event, but a textual memory can retain that the drawer contains the object and that this subtask is complete. Incorrect memory must still be corrected by new evidence.

nodes.title: 实时动作分块
nodes.summary: Enable continuous chunked execution while handling inference delay and cross-chunk consistency.
nodes.definition: Real-Time Chunking addresses the mismatch between slow generative action inference and continuous robot motion. A new flow-policy chunk is generated while an older chunk continues executing, and consistency constraints account for the portion of the old plan that cannot be changed during inference delay. This avoids treating each chunk as if the robot were still at the original observation state. The initial method is an inference-time procedure compatible with existing diffusion or flow policies; a later training-time follow-up is explicitly a separate development.
nodes.example: While the controller executes an existing chunk, the model observes the scene and predicts a replacement. If generation takes several control steps, the replacement must agree with the motion already committed before the switch time. Simply averaging incompatible strategies can produce invalid intermediate motions.
nodes.role_en: RTC connects action-generation models to latency-aware control systems. A faster completion time should be measured end to end, not inferred from token speed or video playback.

nodes.title: SmolVLA 小型视觉语言动作模型
nodes.summary: Provide an efficient open VLA trained on community robot data with an asynchronous deployment stack.
nodes.definition: SmolVLA is a compact open VLA built around a vision-language backbone and a flow-matching action expert. Its design reduces visual token and model computation while using openly shared community robot data. An asynchronous inference stack separates perception/action prediction from action execution to improve responsiveness. The work shows that deployment and data choices matter alongside parameter count. A small model can still require adaptation, compatible observations and careful scheduling; consumer-hardware availability does not imply every task runs at the same latency or success rate.
nodes.example: An affordable arm is given images, joint state and a language instruction. The compact backbone extracts task-relevant features and the action expert predicts a future control chunk. A background inference loop computes the next chunk while the controller executes available actions, subject to the interface’s scheduling assumptions.
nodes.role_en: SmolVLA is an accessible reference for studying flow-based VLA training and systems efficiency. It is useful for controlled comparisons with larger models under matched tasks and hardware.

nodes.title: GR00T N1 通用人形机器人模型
nodes.summary: Provide an open dual-system foundation VLA for generalist humanoid robot skills.
nodes.definition: GR00T N1 uses a dual-system VLA architecture: a vision-language module represents observations and instructions, and a diffusion Transformer produces continuous action chunks. The modules are coupled and trained using heterogeneous data, including real robot trajectories, human video and synthetic sources. The paper targets generalist humanoid manipulation and cross-embodiment learning. High-level visual-language understanding does not itself stabilize a floating-base robot; deployment still needs appropriate body interfaces and lower-level control. Later GR00T releases change models and training recipes and must not be silently treated as the original N1 checkpoint.
nodes.example: For a humanoid bimanual task, language identifies the requested manipulation while cameras and proprioception describe the current configuration. The action model predicts controls through the supported robot interface. Whole-body balance and task action success should be evaluated separately when transferring beyond the demonstrated platform.
nodes.role_en: This is an important bridge between VLA semantics, generative action heads, synthetic data and humanoid deployment. It is a predecessor to the world-action-model formulation in GR00T2.

nodes.title: GR00T 2 基础世界动作模型
nodes.summary: Learn future visual outcomes and actions jointly to support transfer, dexterity and fast adaptation.
nodes.definition: GR00T2 is a foundation world-action model that jointly predicts future video and robot actions using a diffusion Transformer. Joint prediction allows human video and multiple robot interfaces to contribute to a model of physical interaction, while embodiment heads produce executable commands. The official November2026 whitepaper studies cross-adaptation, few-shot learning, dexterity and agentic control. Its reported future video is a model rollout rather than evidence that the real robot has already completed the task. The page also describes a smaller Turbo variant with a whole-body controller interface.

Human-only demonstrations can be evaluated for transfer to a target robot, but task-agnostic target-body data and any subsequent fine-tuning must be recorded explicitly.

nodes.title: Gemini Robotics 机器人模型
nodes.summary: Bring multimodal foundation-model capabilities into robot actions and embodied reasoning.
nodes.definition: Gemini Robotics adapts a multimodal foundation model into a robot action model, while Gemini Robotics-ER provides embodied reasoning capabilities for spatial understanding and higher-level decisions. These are related but different outputs: one produces robot behavior and the other supports reasoning about the environment. The technical report studies generality, dexterity and interactive instruction following across robot tasks. A single brand name does not imply one fully public architecture or a single model performing all low-level stabilization. Evidence should specify the action model, reasoning model and control stack used.

nodes.title: Gemini Robotics 1.5

nodes.title: SuperMimic 可微世界模型全身控制
nodes.summary: Amortize humanoid control learning through one differentiable state world model.
nodes.definition: SuperMimic trains a humanoid motion-tracking policy through short imagined rollouts of a learned differentiable world model. The model fits transitions collected from a standard rigid-body simulator, and policy gradients propagate through the learned predictor rather than through the simulator. Model and policy updates alternate within the training loop. This shares dynamics across many reference motions and provides analytic gradients for policy improvement. The result concerns controller training and motion tracking; it does not replace video-to-motion reconstruction, retargeting, ball perception or task-specific contact planning.
nodes.example: For a G1 reference motion, collect simulator transitions under the current policy. Fit the three-hidden-layer dynamics MLP, then hold its weights fixed inside a policy update and differentiate a short imagined return. A physical G1 rollout evaluates the resulting policy; the learned training predictor need not run as the final motor controller.

nodes.title: BeyondMimic 全身动作跟踪与技能组合
nodes.summary: Connect high-quality motion tracking with flexible cost-guided whole-body control.
nodes.definition: BeyondMimic combines robust motion tracking from human kinematic references with a guided diffusion policy for composing learned motion primitives into downstream humanoid behavior. The tracking stage converts references into dynamically executable motions in simulation and transfers controllers to hardware. The diffusion stage provides task-specific steering using cost guidance rather than requiring a separate specialist for each downstream task. It is therefore broader than only a tracking-training optimizer, while still depending on motion data, robot control interfaces and appropriate sim-to-real evaluation.
nodes.example: A humanoid learns motions that include turns and agile actions. At test time a waypoint cost can guide a shared generative controller toward navigation behavior. The reference motion, simulated tracked motion and physical robot execution are separate artifacts; a clean kinematic preview does not establish dynamic tracking.
nodes.role_en: BeyondMimic supplies an important humanoid-control comparison for SuperMimic. Their stages overlap in tracking, but guided diffusion and downstream composition are not automatically replaced by changing the tracking-training method.

nodes.title: EMMA 多模态自动驾驶模型
nodes.summary: Use a multimodal language-model foundation for multiple autonomous-driving outputs in a shared text representation.
nodes.definition: EMMA is Waymo research on end-to-end multimodal autonomous driving built on a multimodal language-model foundation. Camera inputs are combined with navigation and ego-state context, while trajectories, perception objects and road-graph elements are represented in a unified textual output space. The work studies how shared training across driving tasks transfers foundation-model knowledge to embodied outputs. It is related to VLA ideas but belongs to driving research rather than general robot-arm control. It is distinct from the later Waymo World Model, which is a controllable simulation/generation system.
nodes.example: Given camera views, an instruction to turn and current vehicle status, the model can output a planned trajectory through a language-formatted interface. Evaluating that trajectory on a driving dataset is different from proving safety in live autonomous deployment, and different again from generating sensor data under hypothetical actions.

nodes.definition: A Markov Decision Process specifies states, actions, transition probabilities and a reward objective under a Markov assumption. A partially observed setting additionally separates observations from hidden states. The formalism identifies what information the controller has, how decisions affect future states and what return is optimized. A learned transition model and a learned policy are distinct components of this description.
nodes.example: For a moving cart, state may contain position and velocity while action specifies force. The transition describes its next state, and a reward may penalize target distance. If a camera observes only position, the controller may require a history or state estimate to handle missing velocity.
nodes.role_en: This provides a shared language for model-based RL and goal planning. Reward-free dynamics learning can still use state/action/transition concepts without learning a task-specific reward policy.

nodes.definition: The Bellman equation decomposes expected return into immediate reward and discounted future value. It expresses a consistency relation under a specified policy and transition distribution. Algorithms estimate or enforce this relation using sampled transitions, learned models or dynamic programming. notation.meaning: Actor policy and critic value estimate.

nodes.definition: Actor–critic methods maintain a policy and a value-related estimator. The critic estimates return or advantage information; the actor uses that information to improve action selection. The displayed policy-gradient objective is a general teaching form rather than a universal update rule. Model-based variants can generate training trajectories in a learned model, introducing model error alongside value-estimation error.

A successful actor does not by itself prove that the model predicts arbitrary out-of-distribution actions accurately.

nodes.summary: PPO is a family of policy-gradient methods that restricts the incentive for large updates relative to a policy used to collect data.

nodes.definition: PPO is a family of policy-gradient methods that restricts the incentive for large updates relative to a policy used to collect data. The clipped surrogate uses an action-probability ratio and estimated advantage. It is not a hard guarantee on every measure of policy change. Implementation also requires value estimation, data collection, optimization schedules and appropriate action distributions.

nodes.summary: Predictive uncertainty can reflect variation in outcomes and uncertainty about a model estimated from finite data.

Ensembles compare predictions across several fitted models, but disagreement is not a universal calibrated measure of physical risk. The total-variance identity separates within-condition variation from variation of conditional means; interpreting its components requires an explicit probabilistic model and evaluation.

nodes.title: ROS 2 计算图
nodes.summary: Nodes expose typed interfaces; processes and nodes are different organizational units.
nodes.definition: A ROS 2 computation graph describes participating nodes and their communication interfaces. A node is a named unit of computation, such as a camera driver, estimator, or controller; several nodes may share a process, and one process may contain several execution threads. Publishers, subscriptions, service endpoints, and action endpoints belong to nodes. Discovery finds compatible participants, while an executor schedules callbacks in a client-library application. This graph organizes software communication. It is distinct from a neural-network computation graph, a physical robot kinematic tree, and a SLAM factor graph.
nodes.example: A camera node publishes images, a detector subscribes to them, and a tracker consumes detections. Moving the detector into another process changes deployment and failure isolation, but need not change its topic interface. Record node names, message types, callback execution, and process placement separately when debugging missed updates.
nodes.role_en: Provides the software structure connecting sensors, estimation, learned models, planners, and robot interfaces.

nodes.title: 话题与消息
nodes.summary: Typed publish/subscribe streams carry observations, states, and commands.
nodes.definition: A topic provides asynchronous, typed publish/subscribe communication. Publishers send messages under a topic name; subscriptions receive compatible messages without requiring direct knowledge of the publishing node. A message definition specifies fields and their types. Sensor streams commonly include a measurement timestamp and frame identifier, whose meanings must be preserved through processing. A topic can have multiple publishers and subscribers. Reception still depends on middleware discovery, compatible QoS, scheduling, and network behavior; publishing a message does not establish that a controller received or acted on it.
nodes.example: An image topic carries an image together with its acquisition time and camera frame. A detector publishes bounding boxes with that same measurement time rather than replacing it with inference completion time. A recorder and tracker can subscribe independently, allowing replay without modifying the camera driver.
nodes.role_en: Supplies the transport interface for sensor pipelines, state estimates, and command streams.

nodes.title: 服务与动作
nodes.summary: Services return short request results; actions track long-running goals.
nodes.definition: A service is a request/response interface intended for operations that complete promptly. An action represents a longer-running goal with feedback, a terminal result, and cancellation support. Their interface definitions specify different message sections: request and response for services; goal, result, and feedback for actions. Cancellation is a protocol request whose handling depends on the server; it is not proof of an immediate physical stop. These communication patterns should be selected according to task semantics, with the actuator-level stop behavior implemented and checked independently.
nodes.example: Querying a calibration parameter can use a service. Navigating to a field position can use an action that reports remaining progress and accepts cancellation. If the player cancels navigation, the server transitions its goal state and separately commands a valid stopping behavior through the controller interface.
nodes.role_en: Connects task-level commands and progress monitoring to the continuous sensor and control streams.

nodes.en: DDS and ROS 2 Quality of Service
nodes.title: DDS 与通信质量
nodes.summary: Reliability, history, durability, and timing policies affect whether data arrives usefully.
nodes.definition: ROS 2 exposes middleware Quality of Service policies that configure communication behavior. Common DDS-backed deployments support reliability, history/depth, durability, deadline, lifespan, and liveliness policies. Publishers offer policies and subscribers request policies; incompatible combinations may prevent communication. Reliable transport can retransmit data, while best-effort delivery can discard losses; neither choice guarantees a timely control update. Queue depth and stale-message handling must match whether the application needs the newest observation or every sample. Middleware selection and supported policies should be checked for the actual ROS distribution.
nodes.example: A live camera consumer may prefer recent frames over a growing backlog. A map subscriber may need the most recently published map immediately after joining, motivating suitable durability. Inspect compatibility and message age before blaming an estimator when a topic is visible but delivers no usable measurements.
nodes.role_en: Explains communication failures, stale observations, and queue behavior in deployed perception and control systems.

nodes.title: 坐标变换树
nodes.summary: Transforms must match both the coordinate frame and measurement time.
nodes.definition: tf2 maintains time-buffered transforms between named coordinate frames organized as a tree. A rigid transform converts coordinates of the same physical point between frames. Static sensor mounts use fixed transforms; moving joints or robot poses require time-dependent transforms. A lookup must request a time for which the required transform chain is available. Frame conventions distinguish a locally continuous but drifting odom frame from a globally corrected map frame. An available transform does not establish that its calibration or localization estimate is accurate.
nodes.example: A ball position measured in camera coordinates at exposure time is transformed into base coordinates using the camera-to-base transform at that exposure time. If the head turned during inference, using the latest transform instead can place the ball incorrectly even when its image detection is correct.
nodes.role_en: Connects camera/LiDAR observations, robot kinematics, odometry, maps, and controller targets.

nodes.title: 时钟与同步
nodes.summary: Acquisition time, arrival time, and computation completion are different events.
nodes.definition: A measurement timestamp should identify the physical acquisition event in a defined clock domain. Arrival and processing completion occur later and can vary with transport and computation. Multiple sensors may have clock offsets, drift, exposure intervals, and device-specific stamping rules. ROS time can follow a simulation or replay clock and may pause or jump; a steady clock supports measuring elapsed durations without wall-clock adjustments. Synchronization pairs observations in time but does not remove unknown acquisition delay. Calibration and interpolation must respect these distinctions.
nodes.example: An image arrives after its exposure, while several IMU samples have already arrived. The estimator uses acquisition timestamps to integrate IMU measurements over the image interval. Replaying the same bag with simulated ROS time requires consistent use of that clock, rather than comparing its stamps with the computer wall clock.
nodes.role_en: Prevents incorrect fusion, transforms, latency measurements, and reproducibility during bag replay and simulation.

nodes.title: 控制器与硬件接口
nodes.summary: A read–update–write cycle connects controllers to measured states and command interfaces.
nodes.definition: ros2_control is a ROS 2 framework separating hardware access from controller implementations. Hardware components export state and command interfaces, such as measured joint position and commanded effort. A controller manager coordinates controller lifecycle and interface ownership, while its update loop reads hardware, updates controllers, and writes commands. Supported interfaces, timing, limits, and failure handling depend on the robot plugin and configuration. This framework does not provide a universal stabilizing policy: a humanoid still requires a suitable whole-body controller or learned locomotion policy and a validated hardware integration.
nodes.example: A joint controller reads encoder position and velocity and writes an effort command through a hardware plugin. An upper-level policy may supply position targets instead. The configuration must identify which controller owns each interface, avoid conflicting writers, and verify units and timing before any physical experiment.
nodes.role_en: Bridges software algorithms and robot actuators without conflating a ROS command with realized physical motion.

nodes.title: 相机内参与投影
nodes.summary: Image pixels are rays; metric depth requires additional information.
nodes.definition: A pinhole camera maps a three-dimensional point in its camera frame to image coordinates by dividing its horizontal and vertical coordinates by depth. Intrinsics encode focal lengths and principal point in pixel units. Real cameras require a distortion model, and fisheye lenses may use a different projection family. Calibration estimates model parameters from known geometry and observations. A single pixel generally determines a viewing ray rather than a unique metric point. Depth, stereo, known object geometry, or other constraints are required to recover distance.
nodes.example: A ball center at pixel coordinates is converted into a camera-frame ray after distortion correction. To estimate a ground intersection, the system additionally needs camera pose and a ground-plane assumption. An airborne ball violates that assumption, so image detection accuracy alone cannot establish accurate three-dimensional ball position.
nodes.role_en: Provides the observation geometry used by visual odometry, visual-inertial estimation, reconstruction, and ball localization.

nodes.title: 传感器外参标定
nodes.summary: Sensor measurements need measured transforms into the robot frame.
nodes.definition: Extrinsic calibration estimates the rigid transformation between sensor coordinate frames or between a sensor and the robot body. Rotation and translation must be interpreted with an explicit mapping direction and consistent units. A CAD or URDF mount transform is a geometric specification; calibration tests the actual installation, including mounting errors. Multi-sensor calibration can estimate parameters by minimizing disagreement between observations of common structure. Transform uncertainty propagates into reconstructed positions. Flexing mounts, moving joints, and sensor relocation can invalidate a previously calibrated fixed transform.
nodes.example: Estimate the camera-to-base transform from calibration observations and check it against independent target positions. A small angular error can create a substantial position error at long range. If the camera sits on a moving head, combine its fixed mount calibration with the head joint kinematics at the measurement time.
nodes.role_en: Makes different sensor outputs physically comparable and links perception to robot control coordinates.

nodes.en: IMU Specific Force, Bias, and Integration
nodes.title: 惯性测量与偏置
nodes.summary: Accelerometers measure specific force; bias causes integration drift.
nodes.definition: An IMU combines gyroscope angular-rate measurements with accelerometer specific-force measurements. Specific force is not directly world-frame linear acceleration: gravity and orientation must be handled using the chosen convention. Measurements also contain bias and noise, and biases can vary over time. Integration propagates orientation, velocity, and position between other observations, but its errors accumulate. An IMU alone generally cannot maintain drift-free global position. Noise density, sample rate, saturation, mounting orientation, and acquisition timestamps must be obtained from the actual sensor configuration.
nodes.example: A stationary level IMU typically reports a nonzero accelerometer vector because its support force balances gravity. The estimator rotates the measured specific force into the world frame and adds the world gravity vector to obtain linear acceleration. A small uncorrected accelerometer bias then accumulates into velocity and position error.
nodes.role_en: Supplies short-term motion propagation for VIO, LiDAR-inertial odometry, and robot state estimation.

nodes.en: LiDAR Point Clouds and Motion De-skewing
nodes.title: 激光点云与运动补偿
nodes.summary: A scan contains points acquired at different times, not necessarily one rigid instant.
nodes.definition: A LiDAR measures ranges along emitted directions and produces points in a sensor coordinate frame. Spinning and solid-state sensors have different scan patterns, fields of view, and acquisition timing. A scan assembled while the robot moves contains points measured from different sensor poses. De-skewing uses estimated motion and point timestamps to express those observations at a common reference time. Accuracy depends on timing, extrinsic calibration, scene geometry, and the motion estimate. Reflectivity, occlusion, range limits, and moving objects also affect which returns can constrain robot pose.
nodes.example: A humanoid turns while scanning a wall. Without compensation, the assembled wall can appear bent. Use each point time and interpolated body motion to express points in the scan-start frame. This requires the driver point-time convention and does not remove errors caused by incorrect motion estimates or moving people.
nodes.role_en: Prepares geometrically consistent measurements for scan registration and LiDAR-inertial odometry.

nodes.title: 标定可观测性
nodes.summary: A low residual cannot identify parameters that the recorded motion does not constrain.
nodes.definition: Observability asks whether different hidden states or parameters can be distinguished from the available measurements and motion. Calibration may optimize camera-IMU rotation, translation, time offset, and biases, but some motions leave certain parameters weakly constrained. Linearization exposes this through the rank or singular values of a sensitivity matrix after appropriate gauge freedoms are accounted for. A small fitting residual can coexist with inaccurate parameters. Independent validation, sufficient motion variation, realistic noise assumptions, and parameter uncertainty are therefore necessary when judging calibration quality.
nodes.example: Collecting only nearly static camera-IMU data provides little evidence about time offset because shifting timestamps hardly changes predicted observations. Include controlled rotational and translational variation suitable for the calibration method, then evaluate held-out data. Do not interpret successful optimizer termination as proof that every extrinsic parameter was identified.
nodes.role_en: Explains why calibration and state estimation require informative motion and why some errors persist despite optimization.

nodes.summary: Incremental motion estimates can be continuous while drifting globally.
nodes.definition: Odometry estimates a robot trajectory from successive local motion observations, such as wheel encoders, image correspondences, LiDAR scans, or inertial measurements. Relative transforms are composed to obtain pose over time. Small systematic and random errors accumulate, creating drift. In ROS conventions, an odom frame is locally continuous but may drift without bound; a map frame may receive global corrections and therefore change discontinuously. Odometry, localization against a known map, and SLAM solve related but different estimation problems, and should not be treated as interchangeable outputs.
nodes.example: A robot walks around a closed corridor and local odometry returns near, but not exactly to, its starting pose. The controller can still use the smooth local estimate for short motions. A verified loop closure or external localization measurement can correct global position without making the original incremental estimates error-free.
nodes.role_en: Connects sensor motion measurements to local feedback and provides trajectory constraints for SLAM.

nodes.summary: Jointly estimate motion, gravity-related quantities, and IMU biases from images and inertial data.
nodes.definition: Visual-inertial odometry combines camera observations with IMU measurements to estimate a local trajectory. Images constrain relative geometric motion through feature observations or photometric alignment, while the IMU supplies motion propagation between exposures. Tightly coupled methods optimize or filter these measurements within a joint state containing pose, velocity, and biases. Metric scale can become observable under suitable motion and assumptions, unlike unconstrained monocular visual geometry. Initialization, synchronization, extrinsics, texture, lighting, rolling shutter, and motion excitation strongly affect performance. VIO without global corrections remains an odometry system and can drift.
nodes.example: As a robot turns its head, IMU angular motion helps predict feature movement between images. Reprojection residuals correct the propagated pose and biases. A plain wall or severe blur weakens visual constraints; the IMU can bridge short intervals but cannot supply indefinitely accurate position during visual failure.

nodes.summary: IMU propagation and geometric scan constraints jointly estimate body motion.
nodes.definition: LiDAR-inertial odometry combines inertial propagation with geometric constraints from LiDAR returns. IMU measurements help predict motion and compensate acquisition distortion; point-to-map or feature-based registration corrects that prediction. Tightly coupled approaches estimate pose, velocity, biases, and sometimes extrinsics within a shared estimator. Filter-based and smoothing-based implementations organize computation differently. Performance depends on scene geometry: a long featureless corridor or a sparse distant scene can leave motion directions weakly constrained. A local LIO map does not by itself imply loop closure or globally drift-free SLAM.

In a geometrically repetitive corridor, inspect directional uncertainty and registration failures rather than assuming that a visually dense point cloud determines all six motion dimensions.

nodes.title: 因子图与稀疏平滑
nodes.summary: A factor connects the unknown variables involved in one measurement or prior.
nodes.definition: A factor graph is a bipartite graph with variable nodes and factor nodes. Variables can represent robot poses, velocities, sensor biases, or landmarks. Each factor expresses a measurement likelihood or prior involving a subset of variables. Maximum a posteriori estimation combines these terms; Gaussian error models lead to a weighted nonlinear least-squares objective. Smoothing estimates multiple historical states together, allowing later observations to revise earlier poses. Sparsity comes from local factor dependencies. Gauge freedom, initialization, robust losses, and incorrect associations must be handled; drawing a graph does not resolve them.
nodes.example: A trajectory graph contains one pose variable per selected keyframe. Adjacent keyframes receive odometry factors, and a known landmark adds a measurement factor. Optimizing all these constraints adjusts several poses together. A first-pose prior or another appropriate reference removes the arbitrary global coordinate choice for the selected formulation.
nodes.role_en: Expands the existing SLAM overview into the estimation structure used by smoothing, bundle adjustment, and LIO-SAM.

nodes.title: 地点识别与回环
nodes.summary: Recognizing a place proposes a constraint; geometric verification decides whether to use it.
nodes.definition: Loop closure adds a nonlocal relation between states recorded when a robot revisits a place. Place recognition proposes candidates from visual or geometric similarity; geometric verification checks that observations support a consistent relative pose. A pose-graph or other back-end then distributes the correction across its connected states. Repeated corridors, changing environments, dynamic objects, and perceptual aliasing can create false candidates. Robust estimation can reduce some bad-constraint effects but cannot guarantee correctness. Relocalization recovers pose against an existing map and is related to, but distinct from, closing a trajectory loop.
nodes.example: A robot observes a goal area that resembles the opposite end of a soccer field. Appearance retrieval alone can confuse them. Require geometric consistency and appropriate contextual checks before adding a loop constraint; otherwise the map may be corrected toward the wrong end even though the optimizer converges.
nodes.role_en: Explains how global SLAM corrections extend drifting local odometry and why false loop closures are consequential.

nodes.title: 占据栅格与八叉树
nodes.summary: Free, occupied, and unobserved space have different meanings.
nodes.definition: An occupancy map divides space into cells and estimates whether each cell contains an obstacle. Range observations support occupied endpoints and free space along traversed rays, while unobserved regions remain unknown. Log-odds updates conveniently combine evidence under the chosen inverse sensor and independence approximations. A two-dimensional grid suits some planar navigation tasks; an octree represents three-dimensional occupancy at multiple spatial scales. Resolution, sensor error, moving obstacles, and map aging affect usefulness. Absence of a return is not universally equivalent to free space, especially with range limits or sensor failure.
nodes.example: A LiDAR ray crosses several cells before returning from a wall. The map marks traversed visible cells as free evidence and the endpoint as occupied evidence. Space behind the wall remains unknown. A planner must explicitly choose how to treat unknown space rather than interpreting every unfilled cell as traversable.
nodes.role_en: Connects range measurements and probabilistic updates to collision checking and map-based navigation.
