nodes.en: TSDF and Euclidean Signed Distance Fields
nodes.title: 截断与欧氏符号距离场
nodes.summary: Surface reconstruction and nearest-obstacle distance serve different downstream uses.
nodes.definition: A signed distance field assigns distance values relative to a surface under a stated sign convention. A TSDF fuses truncated distance observations near surfaces and supports reconstruction; its stored values are not generally exact Euclidean nearest-obstacle distances. An ESDF approximates Euclidean distance to the nearest surface and can provide gradients for trajectory optimization. Construction must distinguish observed free space from unknown space, update changed geometry, and select resolution. Planning also needs robot geometry and margins; a positive distance at the robot center alone does not establish collision-free whole-body motion.
nodes.example: A reconstructed wall can be displayed as a mesh from a TSDF. A trajectory optimizer instead queries ESDF distance and gradient at sampled robot body points to penalize nearby obstacles. The body radius or shape, map uncertainty, and unobserved regions remain part of collision-checking assumptions.
nodes.role_en: Provides geometric costs for collision-aware trajectory optimization and local planning.

nodes.title: 导航系统分工
nodes.summary: A navigation stack coordinates estimates, maps, routes, local commands, and recovery.
nodes.definition: A navigation stack combines localization, environmental representations, global planning, local control, and task execution. Localization estimates robot pose; a planner searches for a route; a local controller generates commands using nearby obstacles and motion constraints. Costmaps translate sensed geometry into planning costs, while behaviors or task logic manage failures and goal progression. Nav2 supplies these interfaces and implementations in ROS 2. A mobile-base navigation command does not automatically provide dynamically stable humanoid locomotion: the command must be realized by a suitable lower-level controller, with robot geometry and operating assumptions checked.
nodes.example: A high-level task requests a field waypoint. The global planner selects a route around an obstacle, the local controller issues velocity targets, and a locomotion controller realizes them. A falling risk or invalid localization estimate requires handling across these layers; a successful route search alone does not imply successful physical arrival.
nodes.role_en: Positions SLAM, mapping, classical planning, and learned locomotion within one robotics architecture.

nodes.title: 目标检测与观测几何
nodes.summary: A class label and image box are measurements, not a full physical state.
nodes.definition: Object detection predicts object categories and image regions, often bounding boxes and confidence scores. Detection confidence is not automatically a calibrated probability of metric localization accuracy. A detector may miss occluded objects, confuse similar objects, or produce biased centers. Converting a box or mask into a three-dimensional position requires additional geometry, depth, calibration, or an explicit object model. Training distributions, annotation conventions, and camera conditions affect performance. Detection is a per-observation perception stage; temporal identity, velocity, and uncertainty require additional estimation machinery.
nodes.example: A soccer detector returns a ball box. Its pixel center defines a viewing direction after camera calibration. Estimate distance using validated depth or geometry, and propagate relevant uncertainty. Track errors separately for visible-ball detection, pixel localization, metric position, and downstream control so one success metric does not conceal another failure.
nodes.role_en: Supplies object observations for tracking and interaction while separating recognition from state estimation.

nodes.title: 数据关联与门控
nodes.summary: Determine which observation belongs to which tracked object or landmark.
nodes.definition: Data association assigns incoming observations to existing tracks or landmarks, while permitting new objects, missed detections, and rejected measurements. Motion uncertainty defines a predicted measurement distribution; a Mahalanobis gate rejects observations inconsistent with that prediction. Assignment can also use appearance, class, geometry, and one-to-one constraints. A small residual is not definitive identity evidence when multiple objects are similar or nearby. Incorrect associations can corrupt a tracker or SLAM estimate. Gating thresholds and covariance calibration therefore affect both rejected correct measurements and accepted incorrect ones.
nodes.example: Two balls or ball-like highlights appear near a predicted ball location. Gate candidates using the tracker covariance, then evaluate additional appearance and geometric evidence. If ambiguity remains, retain uncertainty or mark the estimate unreliable instead of silently switching identity and reporting a highly confident velocity.
nodes.role_en: Links raw detections to temporal tracking and feature correspondences used in localization.

nodes.en: Object Tracking, Occlusion, and Ball State
nodes.title: 目标跟踪与遮挡
nodes.summary: Predict state between measurements while exposing uncertainty and model limits.
nodes.definition: Object tracking estimates a temporal state, such as position and velocity, from incomplete noisy observations. A motion model predicts forward; accepted measurements update that prediction. During occlusion or missed detections, uncertainty should grow according to the process model, and the output should identify its observation age. A constant-velocity model is useful over limited intervals but does not describe every bounce, kick, rolling-friction change, or collision. Robot motion must be removed or modeled when interpreting camera-relative measurements. Track persistence and confident physical state are different claims.
nodes.example: A ball disappears behind a leg. The tracker briefly predicts its field-frame position with growing covariance and labels the estimate as unobserved. A later detection is gated before updating. If a kick occurred during occlusion, the old constant-velocity prediction may be wrong and should not be trusted as an observed trajectory.
nodes.role_en: Connects perception to interception, passing, and closed-loop control with explicit visibility and uncertainty.

nodes.title: 观测延迟与补偿
nodes.summary: Control uses a delayed estimate unless acquisition-to-action timing is accounted for.
nodes.definition: End-to-end latency spans acquisition, transfer, queuing, preprocessing, inference, estimation, planning, command transport, and actuator response. Throughput counts completed work per time; it is different from the age of a particular observation when its resulting command acts. Time-stamped state prediction can compensate some delay under a valid dynamics model, but cannot recover unseen events or eliminate prediction error. Tail latency, dropped frames, changing queues, and mismatched clocks matter alongside averages. A measured pipeline budget is needed before claiming that faster inference improves closed-loop behavior.
nodes.example: For an illustrative constant-speed ball moving at two meters per second, a 0.1-second old position differs by about 0.2 meters along its motion. Predicting forward can reduce this offset if velocity is accurate. A bounce during that interval invalidates the simple prediction even when the arithmetic is correct.
nodes.role_en: Links timestamping and tracking to real-time planning, asynchronous inference, and physical action timing.

notation.meaning: Measured observation-to-use delay with compatible clocks.

nodes.title: 实时期限与指令约束
nodes.summary: Bounded timing and actuator limits are separate requirements of a physical control loop.
nodes.definition: A real-time control loop must meet defined timing deadlines, not merely achieve a high average update rate. Worst-case delays, scheduling jitter, blocking operations, memory allocation, and priority interactions can disrupt execution. Command validation separately checks the actuator interface, units, finite values, position/velocity/effort limits, and freshness. A watchdog can transition to a defined fallback when updates stop. Saturation and rate limits alter closed-loop behavior and must be included in controller analysis. These mechanisms reduce specific failure modes but do not prove whole-robot stability, collision avoidance, or comprehensive safety.
nodes.example: A policy produces joint targets faster than the average required rate but occasionally stalls. A watchdog checks elapsed time independently of that average. Each command is checked against configured joint and rate limits before writing hardware. The actual fallback must suit the robot; blindly setting every target to zero may itself be inappropriate.
nodes.role_en: Connects algorithm outputs and latency measurements to enforceable hardware-interface behavior.

nodes.title: 视觉惯性多地图 SLAM
nodes.summary: Feature-based visual, visual-inertial, and multi-map SLAM with place recognition and map merging.
nodes.definition: ORB-SLAM3 is an open-source feature-based SLAM system supporting monocular, stereo, and RGB-D inputs, with visual-inertial configurations and pinhole or fisheye camera models. It combines tracking, local mapping, inertial initialization, place recognition, loop closure, and multi-map management. Maximum a posteriori estimation jointly uses visual and inertial information in its inertial modes. When tracking is lost, the system can create another map and later merge maps when sufficient shared structure is recognized. Its published results apply to specified datasets and sensor configurations, not every robot camera setup.
nodes.example: On a robot head camera, first verify supported image format, intrinsics, camera-IMU transforms, timestamps, and IMU conventions. Evaluate tracking loss, recovery, and trajectory errors under robot motion and field appearance. A successful run on a provided benchmark sequence is evidence about that sequence, not proof that the installed robot is localized reliably.

paper.limitations: Needs calibrated and synchronized inputs. Poor visual information, repeated appearance, dynamic scenes, and aggressive motion can cause failure; recovery is not guaranteed.

nodes.title: 直接激光惯性里程计
nodes.summary: Raw-point scan-to-map registration with an iterated Kalman filter and incremental k-d tree.
nodes.definition: FAST-LIO2 is a LiDAR-inertial odometry framework that directly registers raw LiDAR points against a local map rather than requiring a hand-engineered feature-extraction stage. It uses a tightly coupled iterated Kalman-filter formulation and an incremental k-d tree, ikd-Tree, for map search and updates. The design supports different scanning patterns and emphasizes computational efficiency. It remains a geometric state estimator, rather than a learned image-generating world model. The reported operating rates and motion examples are experimental results under stated hardware and data conditions, not universal robot performance specifications.
nodes.example: To integrate FAST-LIO2 with a robot, confirm the supported LiDAR message format, per-point timing, scan pattern, IMU axes, synchronization, and extrinsics. Replay a recorded route and inspect trajectory, map consistency, processing times, and degeneracy. A dense live point-cloud display alone does not establish globally accurate localization or successful loop closure.
nodes.role_en: Exemplifies filter-based LIO and shows why efficient estimation can use geometry and data structures without a large learned dynamics network.

nodes.summary: Smoothing combines LiDAR odometry, IMU preintegration, and optional global constraints.
nodes.definition: LIO-SAM formulates LiDAR-inertial odometry and mapping with factor graphs. IMU preintegration supports motion prediction and point-cloud de-skewing; LiDAR registration provides corrections that also constrain inertial bias. The framework can incorporate additional information, including GPS and loop closures, when available and configured. Keyframes and local scan-to-submap matching control computation rather than repeatedly registering against an unrestricted global map. This organization contrasts with filter-based LIO while sharing underlying sensor geometry. Correct driver fields, IMU conventions, calibration, timing, and the chosen repository branch remain essential integration details.
nodes.example: Replay a route containing a genuine revisit. First inspect local LiDAR-inertial trajectory quality, then inspect whether a loop constraint was proposed and geometrically valid. Compare trajectory corrections with independent reference data when possible. A visually closed map after optimization can still be wrong if an accepted loop correspondence was incorrect.
nodes.role_en: Exemplifies smoothing-based LIO and the modular addition of local and global measurement factors.

nodes.title: 统一机器人描述格式
nodes.summary: An XML description of named links, joints, geometry and inertial properties.
nodes.definition: URDF is an XML format for describing a robot as named rigid links connected by named joints. A link can contain visual geometry, collision geometry, mass, center of mass and an inertia tensor. A joint specifies its parent and child, joint type, reference transform, motion axis and applicable limits. These fields describe structure and physical parameters; they do not themselves implement walking, perception or a trained controller. A valid robot description must also resolve external mesh paths. Software importing the same file can interpret unsupported extensions differently, so successful parsing is only the first validation step.
nodes.example: For a two-link arm, create two link elements and one revolute joint connecting the parent to the child. Give the joint an origin, an axis and a lower and upper angle. A viewer can then display different joint positions. A physics simulation additionally needs usable inertial and contact properties and a control input.
nodes.role_en: URDF is the entry point for loading G1, Go2 and Booster hardware into kinematics, planning and simulation. Open the linked robot records for pinned source files and audited numeric parameters.

nodes.title: 刚体连杆与附着坐标系
nodes.summary: A link is a rigid component; not every named link is a separate physical moving part.
nodes.definition: A URDF link represents one rigid component and defines a local reference frame. Separate visual, collision and inertial elements may each have their own pose relative to that frame. Fixed joints can attach sensor frames, decorative components or rigidly connected subparts without adding independent motion. Therefore the number of links is not the number of motors or degrees of freedom. Some links serve only as coordinate frames and have no mass entry. For dynamics, the importer must handle these frames consistently, often merging fixed bodies while preserving their transformations and inertial contribution.
nodes.example: The audited G1 29-DoF file has 38 links and 37 joints, of which only 29 joints are revolute. Camera and IMU frames remain useful for interpreting observations even though their fixed attachments add no motor command. Their geometry and inertial data should not be counted twice when fixed bodies are merged.
nodes.role_en: Links provide the reference frames consumed by forward kinematics, camera extrinsics, contact placement and rigid-body dynamics.

notation.meaning: Rotation and translation locating the attached frame.

nodes.explain: A URDF link represents one rigid component and defines a local reference frame. Separate visual, collision and inertial elements may each have their own pose relative to that frame. Fixed joints can attach sensor frames, decorative components or rigidly connected subparts without adding independent motion. Therefore the number of links is not the number of motors or degrees of freedom. Some links serve only as coordinate frames and have no mass entry. For dynamics, the importer must handle these frames consistently, often merging fixed bodies while preserving their transformations and inertial contribution.
nodes.role: Links provide the reference frames consumed by forward kinematics, camera extrinsics, contact placement and rigid-body dynamics.

nodes.title: 关节类型与允许运动
nodes.summary: Joint types constrain relative motion and determine configuration dimensions.
nodes.definition: A joint connects a parent link to a child link and constrains their relative motion. A fixed joint allows no relative motion. A revolute joint rotates about one axis within position limits; a continuous joint rotates about one axis without bounded angle. A prismatic joint translates along one axis. Planar and floating joints represent three and six physical degrees of freedom respectively, although importer support varies. Type alone does not identify a motor: a moving joint can be passive or mechanically coupled. Count joint coordinates, independent motion and independently commanded actuators separately.
nodes.example: A humanoid knee is commonly represented as one revolute coordinate. A wrist decoration fixed to the forearm is a fixed joint, even if its name contains joint. A passive caster may rotate continuously but need no independent motor command. Summing every joint element would overcount all three cases.
nodes.role_en: Joint types determine how URDF coordinates map into forward kinematics, generalized velocities and controller action dimensions.

notation.meaning: Physical motion dimension allowed by the joint type.

nodes.title: 运动学树与闭链
nodes.summary: URDF parent-child connectivity forms a tree; a closed mechanism needs extra handling.
nodes.definition: A kinematic tree has one root link and a unique parent path to every other link. Each URDF joint names exactly one parent and one child, giving a natural traversal for forward kinematics. For a connected tree, the joint count equals the link count minus one. A closed mechanical linkage cannot be represented merely by giving a child two parents in ordinary URDF. Typical workflows choose a spanning tree and express the remaining closure as simulator constraints or a separate mechanism model. A tree that parses successfully can still contain incorrect axes, offsets or inertial parameters.
nodes.example: The audited Go2 file has 42 links and 41 joints, satisfying the connected-tree count. Its four legs branch from the base. If a parallel ankle mechanism is simplified into serial pitch and roll joints, that model must not be mistaken for an explicit simulation of every internal linkage.
nodes.role_en: Unique tree paths support forward kinematics and frame transformations; extra loop constraints connect to constrained dynamics and simulator-specific mechanisms.

notation.meaning: Joints and links of a connected tree.

nodes.title: 原点、平移与欧拉角
nodes.summary: An origin locates one local frame relative to another; joint and inertial origins have different roles.
nodes.definition: An origin specifies a rigid transform with translation xyz and orientation rpy. URDF roll, pitch and yaw use radians and fixed-axis rotations about x, y and z; the equivalent rotation matrix is yaw times pitch times roll for column vectors. A joint origin locates the joint frame in the parent-link frame at zero joint displacement. Visual and collision origins locate geometry inside a link. An inertial origin locates the center-of-mass frame. These transforms are separate: changing a visual origin moves the drawing, whereas changing the inertial origin changes the body's modeled mass distribution.
nodes.example: If a joint origin translates 0.2 m along the parent x direction, its rotation axis passes through that translated joint frame. A center of mass offset 0.05 m above the link origin belongs in the inertial origin; placing it only in the visual origin does not change the dynamics.
nodes.role_en: Origin transforms connect robot descriptions to SE(3), camera calibration, forward kinematics and correct inertia placement.

notation.meaning: Roll, pitch and yaw in radians.

nodes.title: 关节轴与正方向
nodes.summary: The axis is expressed in the joint frame; its sign controls the sign of position and torque.
nodes.definition: A joint axis is a direction expressed in the joint frame, not automatically in the world frame. For a revolute joint it is the axis of rotation; for a prismatic joint it is the direction of translation. Positive rotational displacement follows the right-hand rule. Forward kinematics rotates the axis into other reference frames when needed. Normalize a nonzero axis and verify its direction in a posed model. Renaming a coordinate or copying an axis from another robot does not preserve motion semantics when link frames differ, which matters during motion retargeting and policy deployment.
nodes.example: A joint with axis 0 1 0 rotates about its own y direction. If the joint origin is already rotated relative to the torso, that direction is not the torso y direction. To compare a left and right hip, inspect both their origin rotations and axis signs before copying target angles.
nodes.role_en: Correct axes connect URDF joint positions to Jacobians, inverse kinematics, retargeting and the action sign expected by a motor interface.

notation.meaning: Rotation from the joint frame to the world frame.

nodes.title: 关节限位与物理单位
nodes.summary: Position, velocity and effort limits describe different quantities and are not controller gains.
nodes.definition: The limit element can specify lower and upper position, maximum effort and maximum speed. Revolute positions are radians, revolute velocities are radians per second and revolute effort is torque in newton metres. Prismatic positions are metres, velocities are metres per second and effort is force in newtons. Continuous joints have no finite lower and upper angle requirement. A file's values are model metadata, not a guarantee that every software layer enforces them. Motor thermal limits, torque-speed curves, communication safety checks and proportional-derivative gains generally require additional controller or hardware specifications.
nodes.example: A revolute joint with lower -1, upper 1, effort 40 and velocity 10 permits a modeled angle range of -1 to 1 rad, a 40 N m effort bound and a 10 rad/s speed bound. None of these four numbers specifies the proportional gain of a position controller.
nodes.role_en: Limits bound inverse-kinematics solutions, trajectory optimization, RL action targets and safe command validation. Keep source model values distinct from measured motor capability.

notation.meaning: Joint position, rad for revolute or m for prismatic.
Torque for revolute joints; use force for prismatic joints.

nodes.en: Mass, Center of Mass and Inertia Tensor
nodes.title: 质量、质心与惯性张量
nodes.summary: Mass and inertia set dynamic response; tensor entries must match their frame and units.
nodes.definition: The inertial element contains a mass, a center-of-mass pose relative to the link frame and six independent entries of a symmetric inertia tensor. Tensor entries have units kilogram metre squared and are expressed in the inertial frame about its origin, which URDF uses as the center of mass. For a massive physical body, inertia must be physically realizable: positive principal moments alone are not sufficient; the triangle inequalities also matter. Zero-mass sensor frames need separate importer handling rather than being treated as finite massive bodies. Visual meshes do not automatically supply correct measured inertial parameters.
nodes.example: A 2 kg body with its center of mass displaced from the link origin needs both the correct mass and inertial origin. Simply moving its visible mesh leaves those values unchanged. The audited Go2 file has zero-mass IMU and radar frames with zero inertia; fixed-frame merging differs from simulating them as ordinary massive bodies.
nodes.role_en: Inertial parameters enter manipulator dynamics, centroidal dynamics, balance control and simulator stability. Validate massive-body tensors and preserve total mass when combining fixed links.

notation.meaning: Center-of-mass inertia in kg m squared.

nodes.title: 可视几何与碰撞几何
nodes.summary: Appearance and contact geometry serve different computations and may use different meshes.
nodes.definition: Visual geometry determines how a robot is displayed, including mesh shape and material. Collision geometry determines the shapes used for contact and collision queries. Both have local origins and may use primitives or meshes, but they need not have the same resolution or exact shape. Detailed triangles can increase collision cost; simplified collision shapes change contact locations and can alter learned behavior. A visually plausible foot therefore does not prove that its contact surface is correct. Mesh scale, frame alignment and resource resolution must be verified after import into the target renderer or physics engine.
nodes.example: A foot can have a detailed textured visual mesh and a simple box collision shape. The box bottom defines the simulated support surface. If that bottom is 2 cm above the visible sole, the robot may appear to penetrate the ground even while the contact solver is correctly using its configured shape.
nodes.role_en: Geometry links asset creation to collision checking, simulation contact dynamics, camera rendering and sim-to-real gaps.
nodes.latex: \mathcal G_{\rm visual}\ne\mathcal G_{\rm collision}\quad\text{in general},\qquad d(\mathcal G_1,\mathcal G_2)\le0\Rightarrow\text{contact candidate}

nodes.en: Degrees of Freedom and Actuation Counts
nodes.title: 自由度与驱动数量
nodes.summary: Movable joints, independent coordinates, action dimensions and motors are separate counts.
nodes.definition: A degree of freedom is an independent motion variable. A scalar revolute joint usually contributes one kinematic degree of freedom, while a fixed joint contributes none. Mechanical coupling can reduce the independent count, and passive motion need not have an independent control input. The action vector of a policy may address only a subset of joints or may parameterize targets rather than torques. Consequently a robot record should state its exact file, movable joint types, mimic relationships and actuation evidence. The seven audited examples here have only independent revolute and fixed joints, consistent with their official named body layouts.
nodes.example: G1 mode 11 has 29 revolute joints plus eight fixed joints. Its 29 body coordinates are not 37 motors. If a policy controls only the legs, its action dimension can be 12 while the simulated body still has 29 joint coordinates. Adding a free base increases physical state dimensions without adding six motors.
nodes.role_en: DOF accounting determines model dimensions, retargeting outputs, policy action mappings and comparable hardware descriptions.
nodes.latex: n_{\rm independent}=n_{\rm movable}-n_{\rm dependent},\qquad n_u\le n_{\rm independent}

notation.meaning: Coordinates fixed by independent coupling relations.

nodes.title: 浮动基座与四元数维度
nodes.summary: A free robot has six root-motion DOF, commonly stored with seven pose numbers.
nodes.definition: A mobile robot's root pose is often added by the simulator or a planning system rather than by an explicit floating joint in its URDF. A free root has three translational and three rotational physical degrees of freedom. Storing orientation with a unit quaternion uses four numbers subject to one norm constraint. Therefore a robot with n scalar body joints can have n plus seven generalized position entries and n plus six generalized velocity entries. Quaternion order is a software convention and must be checked at each interface. Body DOF counts in robot product names normally exclude this unactuated free root.
nodes.example: For G1 with 29 scalar joints, a quaternion free-base representation has 36 position entries and 35 velocity entries. Booster's motion CSV stores root position followed by quaternion x,y,z,w before its joint angles. Another simulator may use w,x,y,z. A matching array length does not guarantee a matching orientation convention.
nodes.role_en: Floating-base dimensions connect URDF imports to humanoid state vectors, motion datasets, dynamics and retargeting coordinate conversion.
nodes.latex: n_q=n+7,\qquad n_v=n+6,\qquad q_{\rm root}=(\mathbf p,\mathbf r),\quad \|\mathbf r\|_2=1

nodes.title: 从动关节与被动关节
nodes.summary: A mimic relation is a coordinate dependency; passive means unactuated.
nodes.definition: A mimic joint declares that its position follows another joint through a multiplier and an offset. It therefore usually adds a named moving joint without adding an independent position variable. A passive joint is instead unactuated: it may have an independent motion determined by dynamics and constraints. These concepts must not be conflated. URDF mimic metadata can be understood by a kinematics library while a physics importer ignores it or requires an explicit coupling constraint. Always inspect the importer and actuator mapping rather than inferring controllability from a joint's nonfixed type or from the presence of a mimic element alone.
nodes.example: Two fingers may satisfy right equals negative left plus a fixed offset, leaving one independent opening coordinate. A freely swinging hinge with no motor can still move independently and is passive, not necessarily mimic. None of the seven pinned URDF files audited here contains a mimic element; this does not generalize to their hand-equipped variants.
nodes.role_en: Mimic and passive semantics connect hand models, mechanism constraints, independent-DOF accounting and motion-planning groups.

nodes.title: 传动与电机到关节映射
nodes.summary: Transmission models map actuator motion and effort to joint coordinates.
nodes.definition: A transmission describes the relationship between actuator coordinates and joint coordinates. A simple gear reduction relates motor speed and torque to joint speed and torque, while a differential can couple multiple actuators and joints. Transmission metadata is distinct from joint limits and from a motor controller's gains. Availability and interpretation depend on the control framework and importer. An XML file with no transmission element can still describe actuated hardware if the mapping is configured elsewhere. Conversely a nonfixed joint element is not, by itself, proof of an independently controllable motor or of an available hardware driver.
nodes.example: For an ideal 10:1 reduction, a motor turns ten radians while the output joint turns one radian. Neglecting loss, the output torque is ten times the motor torque. Sign conventions and efficiencies require explicit handling. None of the seven audited robot URDF files embeds a transmission element, so their motor integration must be checked outside these files.
nodes.role_en: Transmissions connect actuator models, hardware interfaces, torque control and correct motor versus joint limits.

notation.meaning: Signed gear reduction under the stated convention.

nodes.title: ROS 2 控制与命令接口
nodes.summary: A robot description can declare command and state interfaces without defining a learned policy.
nodes.definition: ros2_control connects controllers to hardware components through declared command and state interfaces. A ros2_control block identifies a hardware plugin and lists interfaces for joints, sensors or other hardware. A joint might expose position, velocity or effort commands, while measured states are reported separately. The plugin implements the actual communication or simulation backend; listing an interface does not make that backend work. Controller configuration supplies additional behavior such as gains and update settings. The joints referenced by this extension must exist in the robot description. Model-only URDF files may omit these tags entirely and use another runtime integration.
nodes.example: A controller writes a desired joint position into a position command interface while reading measured position and velocity from state interfaces. A hardware plugin exchanges those values with the robot. G1's geometry-only URDF lacking ros2_control tags is still a valid description, but loading it alone does not establish a working robot command channel.
nodes.role_en: Hardware interfaces connect URDF names and units to actual control software, avoiding confusion between a model that renders and a motor that can be commanded.

notation.meaning: Reported states consumed by the controller.

nodes.title: Xacro 参数与模型生成
nodes.summary: Xacro expands reusable XML macros into a concrete URDF for a chosen configuration.
nodes.definition: Xacro is an XML macro system used to generate robot descriptions from reusable components, parameters and conditional choices. A leg macro can instantiate left and right limbs while shared properties specify dimensions or a mesh prefix. The generated URDF is the concrete artifact consumed by many downstream tools. Auditing only the macro source is insufficient because arguments can lock joints, select hands or change inertial properties. Record both the source revision and expansion arguments, then validate the expanded XML. Macro arithmetic also requires unit discipline: a syntactically valid expression can still generate physically inconsistent lengths or masses.
nodes.example: One Xacro source may generate either a fixed-base arm or a mobile robot with sensors. Expand it with the intended arguments, inspect the resulting joint list and compare the model dimensions against the controller. To reproduce an audit, retain the command and arguments together with the source commit and output hash.
nodes.role_en: Xacro connects configurable asset libraries to reproducible URDF variants, avoiding accidental comparisons between different generated robots.

nodes.en: SRDF, Planning Groups and Collision Filters
nodes.title: SRDF、规划组与碰撞过滤
nodes.summary: SRDF adds planning semantics; it complements physical structure in URDF.
nodes.definition: SRDF describes semantics used by motion-planning software alongside a URDF. It can define joint groups, named configurations, end effectors, a virtual connection to the world, passive joints and allowed or disabled self-collision pairs. A group may be a serial chain, a joint collection or a combination of subgroups. These declarations do not replace mass and geometry in the URDF. Disabling a collision pair means a planning system may skip that check, not that the two physical bodies can safely intersect. Check whether a simulator uses the same filters rather than assuming planning and physics collision settings are identical.
nodes.example: Define a left_arm group from shoulder to wrist, then a both_arms group combining left and right arms. A planar virtual joint can connect a mobile root to the world for planning. If adjacent-link collision checks are disabled, document the reason and still inspect unintended collisions involving feet, hands and torso.
nodes.role_en: SRDF connects robot structure to inverse kinematics, motion planning, passive-joint semantics and explicit self-collision policies.
nodes.latex: \mathcal J_{\rm both\ arms}=\mathcal J_{\rm left}\cup\mathcal J_{\rm right},\qquad \mathcal C_{\rm checked}=\mathcal C_{\rm candidates}\setminus\mathcal C_{\rm disabled}

nodes.title: URDF 导入与仿真器语义
nodes.summary: Parsing, rendering and running correct dynamics are different validation stages.
nodes.definition: A simulator compiles a robot description into its own bodies, coordinates, collision shapes and dynamics data. During URDF import it may merge fixed links, discard unsupported tags, approximate meshes or add a floating root through an external setting. Therefore compiled link counts can differ from XML link counts without being wrong. Validate resolved resources, joint order, limits, total mass, base behavior and contact geometry in the target engine. URDF and MuJoCo's MJCF are different formats; an XML extension alone does not identify either one. A successful rendered model is evidence of asset loading, not evidence of a working controller.
nodes.example: The audited G1 URDF has a pelvis root and no explicit floating joint. A locomotion environment must configure a free root during import. If instead it fixes the base, leg motion may render correctly while balance learning becomes a different problem. Inspect the compiled coordinate dimensions and the root's response to gravity.
nodes.role_en: Import validation connects asset descriptions to MuJoCo, Isaac Sim and RL environments while preserving the difference between source parameters and compiled simulation behavior.

Audit the XML rather than reading a DOF number from its filename: locked joints, hands, sensors and coupled mechanisms can change the result. Store movable and fixed joint counts separately, list dependencies, record the root, sum declared masses and sample limits with their units. Cross-check intended actuation against official layout or controller documentation. A URDF mass sum describes this model, including omitted or artificial sensor masses; it is not an independent measurement of the shipped physical robot or its current payload.
nodes.example: G1 mode 10 and mode 11 have 23 and 29 body joints respectively and different wrist and waist configurations. A policy checkpoint trained on one cannot be assumed compatible with the other. The records here pin mode-specific files and distinguish their model mass from product specifications and from a robot carrying an added computer.

nodes.summary: Audited official URDF: 23 revolute + 6 fixed joints; 30 links; XML mass sum 32.10585728 kg.
nodes.definition: This record describes the official Unitree G1 23-DoF body, mode 10 URDF at one pinned repository revision. Parsing finds 23 independent revolute joints, 6 fixed joints and 30 links. The body layout is 12 leg + 1 waist + 10 arm joints. Its declared link masses sum to 32.10585728 kg; this is a simulation-model sum, not a measured product weight. The root frame is pelvis, with no explicit free-root joint. A simulator must decide whether the base is fixed or floating. Check this file's joint names, limits and variant before using retargeted motions or a policy checkpoint.
nodes.example: The joint left_hip_pitch_joint has axis 0 1 0, position bounds -2.5307 to 2.8798 rad, effort limit 139.0 N m and velocity limit 20.0 rad/s in this file. These are source-model parameters. They do not specify PD gains, measured tracking accuracy or motor thermal capability. Open the pinned URDF to inspect all joints.
nodes.role_en: Use this concrete model to connect robot-description concepts to kinematic dimensions, retargeting mappings, simulation assets and hardware-specific controller configurations. Counts and mass are for the exact pinned URDF, not every physical product configuration. Root mobility is configured externally; no explicit floating joint appears. No mimic, transmission or ros2_control elements appear. Mesh assets are linked, not redistributed. Actuation count is inferred from the official named body layout together with independent revolute joint counts; the URDF alone does not certify an operational motor interface.

nodes.definition: A parametric human body model represents a body mesh using a compact set of pose and shape parameters. Pose describes articulated joint rotations; shape describes body proportions. A global translation and orientation place the person in a chosen world frame. This representation makes motion estimated from video or motion capture comparable across frames and subjects. Its skeleton and joint conventions are human conventions, so its parameters are not robot joint commands. Converting the sequence into a robot reference requires an explicit embodiment mapping and coordinate conversion.
nodes.example: An estimated sequence may contain a global pelvis trajectory, rotations for human joints, and a fixed body-shape vector. To imitate it on a G1, first identify the coordinate frame and human joint convention; then solve for robot configurations matching selected body targets.
nodes.role_en: Common interface between monocular human-motion recovery, motion datasets, and retargeting; the human representation can also be bypassed by newer direct video-to-robot methods.

nodes.definition: Motion retargeting computes robot configurations that reproduce selected properties of a source motion despite different limb lengths, joint axes, joint limits, and degrees of freedom. A typical formulation matches body positions or orientations subject to robot constraints. The source and target need consistent reference frames, scale, and anatomical correspondences. Retargeting is usually a kinematic computation: a pose can satisfy its objective while still violating balance or contact dynamics. Physical execution therefore needs motion refinement, a controller, and validation of contact and actuation feasibility.
nodes.example: A human foot target can be reachable for the human but outside the robot leg workspace. A constrained inverse-kinematics solve trades off pelvis, foot, and hand errors while respecting joint limits. Inspect the resulting sequence before using it as an RL tracking reference.
nodes.role_en: Connects human-motion recovery and datasets to robot imitation. It is the explicit conversion stage studied by GMR and an alternative to direct video-to-robot prediction.

nodes.definition: A motion-tracking controller uses the current robot state and a reference trajectory to generate actions that follow the desired body motion. Tracking can include joint angles, body positions, orientations, velocities, and contact events. Reinforcement learning commonly combines tracking rewards with regularization and physical constraints in a simulator. The reference describes desired motion, while the policy determines actions under disturbances and actuation limits. Good tracking of a reference does not establish successful object interaction; ball contact and post-contact recovery need additional task measurements.
nodes.example: For a kicking reference, a controller may track pelvis orientation and foot pose until the strike. A complete trial also checks whether the actual foot reaches the ball, whether the robot remains upright after impact, and whether the ball reaches its commanded destination.
nodes.role_en: Provides the executable low-level controller used by BeyondMimic, motion-guided soccer, teleoperation, and human-video imitation.

nodes.en: Motion Priors: Tracking, Adversarial and Latent
nodes.title: 动作先验：跟踪、对抗与潜空间
nodes.summary: 动作先验：跟踪、对抗与潜空间
nodes.definition: A motion prior restricts or rewards behavior according to demonstrations of plausible movement. Tracking priors reward agreement with a particular time-indexed reference. Adversarial priors learn to distinguish motion transitions from demonstrations and policy rollouts, then supply an imitation reward. Latent priors encode a reusable space of motions that a task policy can command. These approaches differ in how demonstrations constrain timing and behavior. A motion prior encourages properties present in its data; it does not by itself guarantee dynamic stability, object contact, or task success.
nodes.example: A soccer controller can receive a task reward for moving the ball toward a goal and a motion-prior reward for human-like body transitions. Increasing the prior weight changes the tradeoff. Measure ball outcomes and falls rather than treating a natural-looking movement as sufficient evidence.
nodes.role_en: Explains how DeepMimic, AMP, HumanX, humanoid goalkeeping, and soccerbot use human movement differently; these are parallel design choices rather than one mandatory sequence.

notation.meaning: Relative weight of an imitation or style reward.

nodes.summary: 动作质量与物理可执行性
nodes.definition: Motion quality must be checked in several independent dimensions: source fidelity, geometric validity, temporal continuity, contact consistency, and performance under physical execution. A low inverse-kinematics error does not imply feasible torques or stable balance. Foot skating occurs when a supposed stance foot moves relative to the ground; penetration and abrupt joint changes can also enter a retargeted reference. Quantitative checks should accompany complete rendered sequences and closed-loop tests. Report kinematic validation, simulator success, and real-robot execution as separate evidence levels.
nodes.example: For a ten-second motion, plot joint velocity and stance-foot speed, inspect a fixed-camera replay, and then run the controller for the complete duration. A clip that survives a tracking rollout may still have poor source fidelity or unacceptable post-contact sway.
nodes.role_en: Connects GMR reference quality, motion tracking robustness, simulator contacts, and the distinction between reference generation and successful robot deployment.

nodes.title: 球状态估计与可见性
nodes.summary: 球状态估计与可见性
nodes.definition: A soccer controller needs the ball position and often its velocity in a specified frame, even when vision is delayed, noisy, or temporarily unavailable. Camera detections provide image coordinates rather than direct metric state; depth, geometry, or other sensors supply additional constraints. An estimator combines dynamics predictions with timestamped measurements and should expose uncertainty. The sensor setup matters: external motion capture, RGB, depth, infrared reflectance, and LiDAR provide different information. A successful controller under one setup is not evidence of the same autonomy under another.
nodes.example: A ball disappears behind the robot foot for several frames. The estimator propagates its current velocity hypothesis, then corrects the estimate when a new observation arrives. A missed observation and a measured stationary ball must remain different cases in the controller input.
nodes.role_en: Foundation for reactive kicking, interception, active vision, and simulator perception models. Each paper should state which sensors are available at deployment.

nodes.title: 脚球碰撞、踢球与运球动力学
nodes.summary: 脚球碰撞、踢球与运球动力学
nodes.definition: Kicking transfers momentum through a short contact event, while dribbling repeatedly regulates ball motion through intermittent contacts. The outcome depends on relative foot velocity, contact point, foot orientation, ball properties, surface friction, and the robot support state. These interactions can be modeled by impulse and contact constraints or learned through simulation experience. High ball speed alone does not establish a useful kick: direction accuracy, recovery, and repeated execution matter. Simulator parameters and contact timing strongly affect the transfer of these skills to hardware.
nodes.example: A faster swing may increase ball speed while reducing target accuracy or destabilizing the stance leg. Compare complete trials using the same target distance and initial ball distribution, and record shot placement, contact misses, robot falls, and the state after recovery.
nodes.role_en: Physical basis for RoboNaldo, PAiD, dribbling, passing, and goalkeeper contact. Links task rewards to contact simulation and robot dynamics.

nodes.title: 腿式交互中的主动视觉
nodes.summary: 腿式交互中的主动视觉
nodes.definition: Active vision makes sensing direction part of the control problem. A robot can turn its head, neck, torso, or body to retain useful observations while it approaches or interacts with the ball. Visibility depends on camera field of view, occlusion, body pose, and the scene. Training can model those effects or optimize sensor motion jointly with locomotion. This differs from simply attaching a camera to a policy: actions influence what can be observed next, so sensing and movement are coupled through time.
nodes.example: During a sharp dribbling turn, pointing the camera only along the body heading may lose the ball. A policy can coordinate neck rotation and foot placement so that the ball stays observable while changing direction. Hardware actuator range and camera latency still constrain this behavior.
nodes.role_en: Common comparison axis for Dribble Master, Joga, and DAVIS. Their sensor models and real hardware differ, so visibility-aware policies are related rather than identical.

nodes.title: 技能接口与切换状态分布
nodes.summary: 技能接口与切换状态分布
nodes.definition: A skill interface specifies the commands accepted by a low-level policy and the states in which that policy can start and stop reliably. Chaining dribbling, passing, shooting, and recovery requires compatibility between the terminal state distribution of one skill and the initial-state distribution of the next. A valid command format does not guarantee such compatibility. Policies can be trained on states visited by preceding skills, or share a common locomotion substrate. Timing and observation history also matter because the robot may switch while moving.
nodes.example: A shooting policy trained only from stationary starts may fail when invoked mid-stride during dribbling. Collect handoff states from the dribbling controller, train or fine-tune the shot from those states, and evaluate the complete dribble-to-shot sequence.
nodes.role_en: Connects hierarchical soccer planning to executable controllers. Joga uses distributional skill chaining; locomotion-grounded soccer uses a shared locomotion hub; RoboNaldo exposes locomotion and kick-trigger commands.

nodes.title: 多智能体足球与团队协作
nodes.summary: 多智能体足球与团队协作
nodes.definition: Multi-agent soccer introduces other learning or scripted players into a physical control problem. Each agent acts from its own observations, while game outcomes depend on interactions among teammates, opponents, and the ball. Self-play provides changing opponents; population training can reduce overfitting to a single strategy. Team coordination requires more than stable locomotion or accurate kicking, because positioning, passing, and defending operate over longer horizons. Evaluation should separate individual motor skills, one-versus-one play, and cooperative team performance under specified observation and communication assumptions.
nodes.example: Two robots with identical kicking controllers can behave differently when one pursues the ball continuously and the other preserves defensive positioning. Evaluate game outcomes across multiple opponents and seeds, while checking whether perception and communication are local or externally supplied.
nodes.role_en: Links low-level control to the simulated football hierarchy and OP3 one-versus-one self-play. Provides a separate branch for tactics rather than treating tactics as a byproduct of every soccer skill paper.

nodes.title: DeepMimic：示例引导的物理动作控制
nodes.summary: DeepMimic：示例引导的物理动作控制
nodes.definition: DeepMimic trains simulated articulated characters to imitate reference motion while pursuing task goals. The policy observes the character state and reference phase, and reinforcement learning rewards agreement with the example as well as task performance. The method connects motion-capture specification to physical feedback control: disturbances change the actual rollout, and the policy supplies corrective actions. It demonstrates diverse characters and dynamic skills, including recovery. These experiments establish a simulation-based imitation method; a rendered Atlas-like character is not evidence of deployment on a physical humanoid robot.
nodes.example: For a simulated kick, a motion clip specifies the desired style and a task reward specifies the target. Perturb the character during execution and compare its feedback response with direct playback of reference joint angles. Only the former can adapt actions to the altered state.
nodes.role_en: Historical foundation for reference tracking, recovery, and motion-guided robot-soccer curricula. It is a predecessor conceptually, not an assertion that every later system reuses its exact implementation.

nodes.title: AMP：对抗动作先验
nodes.summary: AMP：对抗动作先验
nodes.definition: AMP learns a motion-style reward from demonstration transitions rather than requiring the controller to follow one predetermined clip and phase. A discriminator separates demonstration transitions from policy-generated transitions, and its output supplies an imitation signal during reinforcement learning. A task reward still specifies what the character should accomplish. This enables unstructured motion datasets to guide style without explicit clip selection. The original work evaluates physics-based simulated characters; later humanoid soccer methods adapt the adversarial-prior idea to robot embodiments and interaction tasks.
nodes.example: A dataset contains running and turning transitions. A soccer policy receives a ball-progress task reward and an adversarial style reward. It can choose movement transitions according to the task rather than advancing through one fixed running clip.

nodes.explain: AMP learns a motion-style reward from demonstration transitions rather than requiring the controller to follow one predetermined clip and phase. A discriminator separates demonstration transitions from policy-generated transitions, and its output supplies an imitation signal during reinforcement learning. A task reward still specifies what the character should accomplish. This enables unstructured motion datasets to guide style without explicit clip selection. The original work evaluates physics-based simulated characters; later humanoid soccer methods adapt the adversarial-prior idea to robot embodiments and interaction tasks.

nodes.title: PHC：持续动作跟踪与跌倒恢复
nodes.summary: PHC：持续动作跟踪与跌倒恢复
nodes.definition: PHC addresses continuous reference-driven control of simulated humanoid avatars when reference poses are noisy and unexpected falls occur. Its progressive multiplicative control policy adds capacity to learn harder motions and recovery without discarding previously acquired skills. The controller can continue following references rather than requiring a reset after every failure. This is especially relevant when motion originates from video estimation or generated motion instead of a clean capture sequence. The system concerns physical simulation of avatars; robust simulated recovery does not establish the same behavior on a real G1.
nodes.example: Feed a noisy video-estimated pose sequence into the simulated controller, disturb the avatar, and observe whether it recovers and resumes tracking. Evaluate both recovery and reference error over the uninterrupted sequence rather than terminating at the first fall.
nodes.role_en: Reusable foundation for large motion libraries, recovery policies, and noisy human-motion interfaces; PHC is also one retargeting baseline considered by GMR.

nodes.title: GVHMR：重力视角坐标下的人体动作恢复
nodes.summary: GVHMR：重力视角坐标下的人体动作恢复
nodes.definition: GVHMR recovers human motion in a world coordinate system from monocular video. It predicts poses in a gravity-view coordinate system defined by gravity and the camera viewing direction, reducing ambiguity associated with arbitrary world orientations. Camera rotations then transform the estimates into world-grounded motion. Per-frame pose estimation avoids the same autoregressive accumulation mechanism as methods that repeatedly predict relative pose updates. The output is human motion suitable for downstream processing, not an executable robot controller; camera and motion-estimation errors can propagate into retargeting.
nodes.example: A moving-camera soccer video contains both camera motion and a person’s kick. Recover a world-grounded human sequence, inspect its ground alignment and global trajectory, and then retarget it. A plausible camera-view overlay alone does not verify the world trajectory or robot balance.

nodes.title: GMR：通用动作重定向与参考质量
nodes.summary: GMR：通用动作重定向与参考质量
nodes.definition: Retargeting Matters systematically studies how the quality of human-to-robot reference motions affects downstream humanoid tracking. Its General Motion Retargeting method maps multiple human motion formats to diverse robot embodiments with inverse-kinematics-based processing. The evaluation holds the BeyondMimic tracking setup comparatively fixed to isolate retargeting effects instead of allowing extensive reward tuning to hide reference defects. Foot sliding, penetration, and infeasible movement can reduce robustness even when many frames appear plausible. The retargeter produces references; the tracking policy supplies physical feedback actions.
nodes.example: Retarget the same LAFAN1 sequence with different methods and train trackers under matched settings. Compare source fidelity, contacts, complete sequence success, and recovery. An accurate-looking isolated frame cannot establish that a long dynamic reference is executable.
nodes.role_en: The requested General Motion Retargeting branch; separates kinematic reference conversion from policy tracking and links directly to BeyondMimic and TWIST.

nodes.title: TWIST：全身动作模仿遥操作
nodes.summary: TWIST：全身动作模仿遥操作
nodes.definition: TWIST builds whole-body humanoid teleoperation around human motion imitation. It first retargets motion-capture sequences into robot references and then learns a unified whole-body controller with reinforcement learning and behavior cloning. Its analysis distinguishes privileged future reference information available during training from the signals usable by a responsive deployed controller. The resulting system covers locomotion, legged manipulation, whole-body manipulation, and expressive motion. Teleoperation supplies the intended movement; robust reference execution is not the same problem as autonomous task planning or language-conditioned decision making.
nodes.example: A human operator changes from walking to a whole-body reaching movement. The retargeting interface converts the human pose into a robot reference, and the controller tracks it while maintaining physical feedback. Check reference latency and whether the deployed policy uses future frames.
nodes.role_en: Concrete path from GMR and imitation learning to real humanoid control; useful for collecting robot demonstrations for later autonomy.

nodes.summary: HumanX：从人类视频学习交互技能
nodes.definition: HumanX converts short human videos into robot interaction skills through two coordinated components. XGen builds anchor-centric interaction data and augments it to expand plausible robot-object configurations. XMimic emphasizes interaction-critical parts of imitation when learning the controller. The framework targets anchorable interactions rather than assuming any arbitrary video can directly become an executable policy. The October 2026 abstract reports nine skills across basketball, football, badminton, cargo pickup, and reactive fighting with zero-shot G1 transfer. Task-specific external sensing assumptions must still be read for each demonstration.
nodes.example: For a demonstrated ball interaction, preserve the relation between the striking body part and the ball while varying admissible starting configurations. Evaluate the learned controller on new interaction states and complete exchanges. A successful open-loop shot and a perception-conditioned passing exchange are different tests.
nodes.role_en: Connects recovered human motion, contact-preserving augmentation, and humanoid soccer interaction. The current v2 reports nine skills; counts in older project material may differ.

nodes.definition: BeyondRetarget studies a direct route from monocular RGB video to robot motion. Instead of requiring an explicit estimated human body sequence followed by a separate retargeter, it learns robot-oriented implicit representations and applies contact-aware motion optimization. This design aims to reduce errors that become fixed when human-motion estimation and retargeting are separate stages. The paper reports simulation and real humanoid execution comparisons. Its generated motion still needs a controller and physical evaluation; bypassing a human representation does not eliminate monocular ambiguity or robot constraints.
nodes.example: Compare two pipelines on the same video: human recovery followed by GMR, and direct robot-motion prediction. Check contact continuity, reference accuracy, latency, and complete controller execution. A lower prediction loss does not by itself establish better balance or safer impact behavior.
nodes.role_en: Alternative branch to the GVHMR-to-GMR pipeline. It changes the representation and optimization boundary rather than replacing the need for robot physics or tracking.

nodes.en: From Motor Control to Team Play in Simulated Humanoid Football
nodes.title: 分层学习：从运动控制到模拟团队足球
nodes.summary: 分层学习：从运动控制到模拟团队足球
nodes.definition: This work integrates imitation learning, individual reinforcement learning, multi-agent reinforcement learning, and population-based training into physically simulated humanoid football. Learning proceeds across temporal scales: low-level natural movement supports intermediate ball skills, which support team behavior over longer horizons. Transferable behavioral representations connect these stages. The contribution is the integration of motor control and coordinated decisions rather than a new camera-based ball detector or physical humanoid deployment. Its avatars operate in a simulated multi-agent setting; hardware and egocentric perception claims should not be imported from later robot soccer systems.
nodes.example: Compare a policy trained only to move naturally with one trained to dribble and then play with teammates. Running quality, ball skill, and team decisions need separate measurements. A goal can depend on teammate positioning even when the individual motor controller is unchanged.
nodes.role_en: Soccer research branch: Integrated learning at movement, skill, and team-decision timescales.

nodes.en: Learning Agile Soccer Skills for a Bipedal Robot
nodes.title: OP3：深度强化学习的一对一足球
nodes.summary: OP3：深度强化学习的一对一足球
nodes.definition: This work trains a miniature humanoid with twenty actuated joints to play a simplified one-versus-one soccer game. Reinforcement learning produces locomotion, turning, kicking, fall recovery, and basic game-dependent behavior that transfer from simulation to physical OP3 robots. Skill reuse and multi-agent learning connect robust movement to longer-horizon game objectives. The setup is important: the original real-game state information includes an external motion-capture system, so it should not be described as fully onboard vision-only soccer. Robot size, control rate, and task definition also differ from full-size G1 systems.
nodes.example: Observe a robot fall, recover, pursue the ball, and block an opponent within one game. Evaluate both recovery and scoring against matched opponents. The result does not imply that the same network can run unchanged on a G1 or perceive the ball from its own camera.
nodes.role_en: Soccer research branch: Real miniature-humanoid soccer with learned agile skills, recovery, and basic tactical behavior.

nodes.title: DribbleBot：自然地形中的四足运球
nodes.summary: DribbleBot：自然地形中的四足运球
nodes.definition: DribbleBot learns dynamic ball manipulation while a quadruped walks over varied natural terrain. Policies train in simulation and transfer to a real robot with body-mounted cameras and onboard computation. The task couples locomotion to ball dynamics, so varying ground interaction and sensing conditions are central rather than incidental disturbances. It provides a useful predecessor for active sensing and robust dribbling in humanoid systems, while its four-legged support geometry changes balance and contact possibilities. Its demonstrations do not establish that an identical policy or reward design transfers directly to a biped.
nodes.example: Train the same commanded ball-velocity objective over different surface parameters. A controller must adapt both body movement and contact timing as the ball slows differently on grass and sand. Evaluate actual ball motion rather than only the robot’s walking velocity.
nodes.role_en: Soccer research branch: In-the-wild quadrupedal dribbling with onboard sensing and computation.

nodes.definition: This quadrupedal goalkeeping framework separates rapid ball interception into low-level agile locomotion skills and a high-level motion-planning policy. Different skills cover different parts of the goal, while the planner selects a skill and its movement parameters according to the incoming ball. The task tests fast nonprehensile interaction rather than ordinary velocity-command locomotion. Real Mini Cheetah experiments support the approach under the authors’ sensing and field setup. The work is a useful predecessor for humanoid goalkeeping, whose biped support and human-motion objectives introduce different constraints.
nodes.example: An incoming trajectory reaches the left side of the goal. The planner chooses an appropriate saving skill and target, and the low-level controller executes it within the available time. Evaluate interception and recovery rather than only whether the robot reaches a target pose.

nodes.summary: SoccerDiffusion：从比赛记录学习端到端动作
nodes.definition: SoccerDiffusion learns humanoid soccer control from recordings of real RoboCup gameplay. A Transformer-based diffusion model predicts joint-command trajectories from multimodal observations that include vision, proprioception, and game state. Distillation reduces the iterative diffusion process to a single inference step for embedded execution. The reported system imitates behaviors such as walking, kicking, and recovery in simulation and on robots. Its learned tactical ability remains limited, so reproducing low-level recorded behavior should be distinguished from learning a complete competitive game strategy.
nodes.example: A recorded observation window contains camera input, joint state, and game context. The model generates a short action trajectory, and a distilled student executes a faster approximation. Compare rollout stability and response latency, then separately test whether the policy chooses appropriate game behavior.
nodes.role_en: Soccer research branch: Gameplay imitation with a diffusion controller and single-step distillation.

nodes.summary: Dribble Master：从步行到主动感知运球
nodes.definition: Dribble Master uses a two-stage curriculum to learn humanoid dribbling. The robot first learns locomotion and then adapts the policy for ball manipulation. A virtual camera model exposes training to field-of-view and perception restrictions, while rewards encourage sensing behavior that retains the ball in view. nodes.definition: Humanoid Goalkeeper learns a single policy for rapid whole-body interaction with incoming balls. nodes.definition: RoboNaldo uses a single human-kick reference as an initial scaffold and progressively shifts reinforcement learning toward shot outcomes. Its curriculum learns a stable kicking prior, adapts to stationary balls at varied positions, and extends to moving-ball shooting through locomotion commands and a kick trigger. nodes.definition: Joga is a full-stack G1 soccer system for dribbling, shooting, passing, and receiving. A custom two-degree-of-freedom torso-mounted neck lets the policy coordinate gaze with body movement. A learned perception alignment model reproduces detector errors, while a whole-body unsupervised actuator network corrects simulator joint-target behavior using short hardware recordings. Skill policies train with aligned perception; dribbling is further refined with actuator corrections. Distributional skill chaining prepares passing and shooting for the states actually encountered during dribbling, enabling transitions while the robot is moving.
nodes.example: During a dribble-to-shot transition, the body and neck policy maintains ball visibility and the shot begins from a state produced by dribbling. Compare the nominal simulator with perception-aligned and actuator-aligned versions using the same commanded turns and complete hardware trials.

nodes.definition: This method begins with a general command-conditioned locomotion controller and adds motion-guided kicking skills as task-gated layers. Each skill starts from and returns to the same commandable locomotion state, making locomotion a shared hub for composition and recovery. It explicitly evaluates gait capability alongside shooting rather than assuming locomotion is adequate because an approach succeeds. The reported G1 library contains seven kicks with varied directions, including lateral and rearward strikes. This is a modular alternative to deriving all movement from a single tracked kick reference.
nodes.example: A controller walks sideways, invokes a lateral kick, and returns to commanded locomotion. Test command tracking, terrain response, push recovery, and shot placement with the full library enabled. The common return state reduces the number of pairwise transitions that must be specially trained.

nodes.en: VideoMimic: Visual Imitation Enables Contextual Humanoid Control
nodes.title: VideoMimic：利用环境上下文的视觉模仿
nodes.summary: 从单目视频重建人体与环境，再学习环境条件的全身控制。
nodes.definition: VideoMimic is a real-to-sim-to-real pipeline for learning environment-dependent humanoid skills from everyday monocular videos. It jointly reconstructs the human movement and the surrounding scene, converts that reconstruction into simulator-ready context and robot references, and learns a whole-body policy. The policy is conditioned on the environment and global root commands, allowing movement to depend on stairs, seats, and other relevant geometry. Its real-robot demonstrations include stair ascent and descent and sitting or standing. Human reconstruction, environmental reconstruction, retargeting, and feedback execution remain distinct stages with different error sources.
nodes.example: A video of a person sitting on a bench contains both a body trajectory and the bench geometry. Recover their relative arrangement, retarget the movement, and train in the reconstructed scene. At deployment, evaluate complete sitting and standing sequences, including contact and final balance.
nodes.role_en: Adds environment-aware visual imitation to the motion branch. This is the verified VideoMimic paper, not an inferred expansion of the unresolved name BioMimic.
